> *v2 note (2026-07-25):* this revision incorporates the **2026-07-24/25 universalization** — the three axes (methods · modes · levels), the call-lead-time ladder with scaffold fading, the three-tier scoring architecture and the implied point, the two speaker formats, the local-first system architecture and the ball's reduced job, the classroom channel and the icebreaker-slot reframe, and place-sponsorship. Claims grow from ten to sixteen and pre-registrations from three to five. The v1 claims are unchanged in substance; §§3.1, 4.1, 5.1, 5.2, 7.1, 9.1, 9.2 are new, and §§11–12 are extended. The prior-art clock for the v1 claims runs from the 2026-07-23 push; for the v2 claims, from this one. *(Superseded in part on 2026-07-27 — see the note below; the two speaker formats described here became three, and the claim count moved again.)*
>
> *v3 note (2026-07-27):* this revision adds the **seat taxonomy and the two delivery mechanisms that were ratified but never written**. §3 is resorted from four seats to **five, in two classes** — *determined* (caller, equalizer), whose outputs are pure functions of declared inputs and are checkable by recomputation, and *judged* (umpire, witness), whose outputs are perceptions and are checkable only by one-sentence explanation — with the **seat-migration bar** governing both directions. New **§4.2** establishes the caller as deterministic given roster and seed, from which auditable fairness, count-only multi-device agreement, and the absence of per-participant state all follow. **§5.2 grows from two speaker formats to three named ones — Relay, Call, Free** — the relay call having been absent from the specification while it was already the format intended to ship; the pilot constraint is accordingly restated by property (*a trial must run a caller-on format*) rather than by position in the list. The abstract now leads with the relay rather than the mesh, and **P-S5 gains its stated precondition** (a device available at recess, no instruction given), without which a null result cannot distinguish an unpopular game from an absent device. Claims grow from sixteen to **nineteen**. **The prior-art clock for claims 17–19 runs from this push**, not from either earlier one; §§1–11 claims are unchanged in substance.
>
> *v7 note (2026-08-13):* a **floor correction, and the rare one where the shipped product was ahead of the paper.** The implementation has been running Call at three players while this document said four globally. §3's *Why four is the floor* is replaced by *Why the floor moves with the format*: the surprise condition (three receivers) is restated **once** as an invariant, and the only variable — whether a body is spent on calling — supplies **Relay 4, Call 3**. No claim is added; a variable that was always implicit in the derivation is made explicit. ⚠️ This does **not** reinstate the per-mode minimum table withdrawn in v6, and it does **not** close the open Team-format question, which is named in §3 rather than left to silence.

*v4 note (2026-07-27):* a **title and abstract correction, no claims change.** The paper was titled *"An AI-Called Circulation Sport"* when the caller was understood as an intelligent intermediary. The v3 seat taxonomy and §4.2 established the opposite — the caller is a **determined** seat, a pure function of roster and seed, checkable by recomputation and explicitly not a judgement — with the result that the title asserted of the mechanism precisely the property the design had given up in order to make its fairness auditable. Two further readings had gone stale beneath it: the shipping delivery format (**the relay call**, claim 19) puts a *human* voice on the announcement, and the arrival of speech synthesis as a pronunciation fallback in the reference implementation gives "AI-called" an available reading — *called in a synthetic voice* — that was never its sense. The title now reads **"An Impartially-Called Circulation Sport for the AI Age"**: the *property* rather than the technology, on the same reasoning §4.2 gives for determinism itself — an implementation-independent property outlives the implementation that first carried it. The abstract gains the determinism sentence that justifies the new adjective. **The coined term "AI-called circulation sport" remains coined and freed in §3 and is retained in the keywords**, together with the patent-class phrase §10 names — retitling does not un-free a term, and the dedication's defensive reach comes from the disclosure rather than from the title. *"For the AI Age" is unchanged and means what it always meant: the era whose abundances the sport is designed to spend (§1), not a claim about what runs the caller.* Also corrected: the abstract said **sixteen** claims after the v3 pass took the count to **nineteen**.
>
> *v5 note (2026-07-27):* **a change of spine, not of specification.** Through v4 the paper derived the sport from an *abundance* — machine intelligence lifting the officiating, matching, and witness scarcities under which all previous sport was designed — and the caller mechanism followed as a way to spend it. That derivation is engineering, and it left the paper unable to answer why the abundance should be spent this way rather than another. The premise is now stated first and the abundance demoted to its enabling condition: **a name spoken aloud is an address, an address requires someone other than yourself, and the sport exists to distribute that address equally.** §1 is rewritten around it, opening on Carnegie's maxim and inverting it (offered as a technique for advantage; kept here for the recognition, with the advantage engineered out, since nobody chooses whose name is said), with the own-name attention literature supplying the narrower empirical leg that §11 is careful to distinguish from the broader claim. Every mechanism in §§3–8 is unchanged; several are now *derived* rather than asserted — equal-yet-random, the impartial caller, the absence of per-participant statistics, and the dyadic point all follow from the premise in four lines. **New §5.3 states the constraint the premise forces and the prior specification violated: no participant may be called in their own voice.** A system holding participant-recorded name audio for pronunciation will reach for it at call time and deliver each player a recording of themselves — not a poor address but *no address at all*. §5.3 separates the two speech acts a single artifact had been performing (the pronunciation, which belongs to the name's owner; the call, which necessarily does not) and specifies the transfer between them; **Call accordingly speaks every name in one uniform voice**, which is claimed as a property rather than conceded as a limitation, since a uniform channel addresses all participants identically. Claims grow from nineteen to **twenty-one**; **the prior-art clock for claims 20–21 runs from this push.** P-S6 pre-registers the premise itself with two named counter-hypotheses (habituation; celebration), publish-either-way. Two honest limits are added and are the paper's most exposed: the address premise is *asserted, not measured*, and the uniform synthetic voice satisfies the constraint's letter — it is an other — while only partly satisfying its spirit, since it is not a person who spent attention on you. That gap is handled by ranking the formats (**Relay remains the default; Call is the device-plentiful case**) rather than by pretending it closes. §5.3 also specifies the gap's partial repair, added at founder request in the same pass and **claimed as claim 22: the cross-recording chain**, in which each participant records one *other* participant's name — the circle called in its own voices, with the naive form of that idea (playing each participant their own recording) barred by the constraint and the intuition preserved by inverting the implementation. Two persona references are corrected as stale in the same pass: the call is the bare name, carrying no speaker-attribution prefix — which the address premise independently requires, since a prefix names a speaker who does not exist —  and the rabbit mascot no longer teaches this sport.

> *v6 note (2026-07-30):* **one correction the paper owed itself, one new mechanism, and the accumulated backlog folded in.** The correction first, stated rather than tightened quietly: §4 and claim 3 gave the equal-distribution guarantee **over a session**, and a session is a *prefix* of a round — so the published wording **overstated what the mechanism delivers**, and §2's classroom scene described precisely the case that fails. Both now read **over a complete round**. The reference-implementation defect that surfaced this — a caller whose progress reset each session, so that a class of thirty running a ten-minute warm-up called the same ten children every day and never called the other twenty — is specified as new **§4.3** and **claim 23, round continuity via circle-scoped progress persistence**: the mechanism that makes claim 3 reachable under real usage, and one whose absence **no session-level test detects**, since within any one session the distribution is exactly correct. **The prior-art clock for claim 23, and for amended claim 3, runs from this push.** Also corrected: **the player minimums**, written before the relay format and silently assuming the caller was not a person. The abstract and §3 said *one to N players* and §3.1 gave per-mode minimums as low as one — while a human relay caller is a person who is not receiving, which makes a circle of one impossible in the very format this paper names as its default. The floor is **four**, now stated once in §3 with its reason, and the per-mode minimums are **withdrawn rather than restated**, so that one number cannot drift out of step with another. New material, none of it changing an existing claim: **§6 gains the two difficulty dials** — the circle's radius, and method restriction read upward — with the *declare what, never why* guard, whose sharpest risk is accessibility rather than fairness (a legible difficulty badge invites a circle to read a body as a declaration); these had shipped to the CC0 rules and never reached the specification, a drift running product→paper rather than the usual direction. **§5 states what the two arrows actually do** — they relocate the opponent, from a person, to the drop, to the circle's own earlier state. And **§9.1 adds P-S7 and P-S8**, which test the premise *beneath* the mission rather than the sport, and which can be run without the sport at all: if P-S7 fails, this sport may pass every other prediction here and still be a well-made game with no mission. Claims grow from twenty-two to **twenty-three**; pre-registrations from six to **eight**. **Added in the same pass, after a literature check the previous draft of P-S7 had gestured at without performing:** §10 now surveys **the name-and-belonging literature** and states plainly which side of the relation it sits on — Cooper et al. (2017) on *perceived* instructor knowing, Kohli and Solórzano (2012) on mispronunciation as racial microaggression, Walton and Cohen (2011) as the outcome-side evidence that belonging moves at all, and Goodenow (1993) as the instrument P-S7 and P-S8 specify rather than invent. **All of it runs teacher → student**, and the authors are aware of no controlled study of *student-to-student full-coverage* name knowledge — which is P-S7's actual subject, stated as a gap rather than a discovery. §13 also gains a **flourish, explicitly marked as one**: the Khmer សី sounds like the English *say*, the two are unrelated, and the paragraph carries its own deletion test.
>
> *Draft notes for the editor:* paper №1 of the July 2026 **games-doctrine sprint** (three papers, one day's ratifications, 2026-07-23). Claims division with siblings, stated for the record: the present paper owns the **sport** — the caller mechanism and the rule architecture of B-Sey™. Its same-sprint companion *The Wager That Isn't* owns the **challenge/stake/pot grammar** (B-Match℠) that nests on this sport's net mode; the third sprint paper *The Game That Graduates You* owns the **third-party game-client doctrine** (the witness API). All three share one organizing principle, coined and freed in the present paper: **the play/currency wall** — *competition and play may generate the story; only witnessed giving moves the currency.* Earlier corpus publications are cited, not re-claimed: *Need-Compiled Questlines* owns the mints-nothing quest class; *Proof of Coordinate* owns the individuation primitive the ball's chronicle uses. The sport is design-complete and unbuilt (founder-ratified across 2026-07-23, including the same-day B-Ball→B-Sey rename); every claim is architectural, strata-dated to the design layer. The prior-art clock starts at this markdown push. Compact sprint draft; density pass = editorial option.

---

## Abstract

A name spoken aloud is not a sound but an **address**, and an address requires someone other than yourself. Carnegie's maxim — that a person's name is the sweetest sound in any language — reads as a fact about acoustics and is really a fact about *attention*: what a remembered name proves is that another person spent some on you and kept it. This paper takes that as a design premise and asks what a game would be if it guaranteed the sweetest sound to every participant equally, removed the choice of whom to address from human hands entirely, and refused to let the address become a rating. The derivation is tight: **everyone addressed** (equal-yet-random distribution), **nobody choosing** (an impartial caller), **no evaluation** (no per-participant statistics anywhere in the system), **the address completed** (a dyadic scoring unit credited to no individual), and — the consequence a naive implementation gets wrong — **no participant ever called in their own voice**, because a recording of yourself saying your own name is not an address but a mirror.

The guarantee was unbuildable until recently, which is the second half of the problem. Every sport in history was designed under three scarcities. **Umpires are scarce**, so games tolerate bad calls, and the figure of the referee absorbs abuse so chronic it is now collapsing youth-sports officiating in multiple countries. **Fair opponents are scarce**, so sport is organized as segregation infrastructure — by age, sex, size, and skill — and the one social unit that most needs shared play, the mixed-age family, is precisely the unit no sport accommodates. **Witness is scarce**, so games keep score of *persons*, and the counting hardens into statistics, rankings, and fame hierarchies — the attention economy's atom, present at the playground. Machine intelligence ends all three scarcities at once. A sport *designed for* that abundance — rather than an old sport with cameras added — can spend it on what the scarcities stole: inclusion, giving, and story. The order of the two halves is load-bearing and easy to invert: **the address is the premise and the lifted scarcities are the enabling condition.** An impartial announcer is worth building only if there is a reason every person present should be named aloud.

This paper specifies such a sport. **B-Sey™** is a circle game descended from the Southeast Asian *sey* (Khmer សី, the dusk game of collective keep-alive), played by **four or more in Relay and three or more in Call** with foot or paddle, with or without a net, cooperatively or adversarially — and organized by one mechanism with no precedent in sport: **the caller**. A machine intermediary announces, before each strike, the *name* of the player who must receive next — distributing touches **equally yet randomly**, so that participation is egalitarian, attention is universal (anyone's name may be next), and, as a structural by-product, *strangers learn each other's names through play*. That selection is not a judgement but an **arithmetic**: the receiver sequence is a pure function of the roster and a seed declared before play, so any participant may recompute a finished session and confirm that nobody was skipped and nobody was protected. The sport's central fairness property is therefore *audited rather than trusted* — which is why this specification calls the sport **impartially**-called rather than AI-called, a distinction §4.2 makes structural. Because the caller designates receivers on both sides of the net, targeting a weaker opponent is not merely discouraged but **absent from the game's move-set** — to the authors' knowledge the first net sport in which exploiting the weakest human present is structurally impossible. The point is **dyadic** — it increments on successful *receipt*, so every score is a completed give-and-receive and no one scores alone. Handicaps are applied **at the start line, never in the stream**: unequal teams begin at unequal countdown numbers on a coarse fixed lattice (multiples of three), a quantization that makes the handicap read as a garment size rather than a skill rating. Cooperative play counts *up* (the collective streak); adversarial play counts *down* to zero — first to nothing wins. The announcement reaches the circle in one of three named formats, of which the default — **the relay call** — speaks the name *privately to a single rotating human*, who calls it aloud: fairness stays machine-held while delivery is human, so the sport runs on **one borrowed device** with no loudspeaker, no network, and no clock synchronization, and the rotating relay is where participants practise *producing* the names they otherwise only hear. Where devices are plentiful, a **synced-device mesh** speaks the call in unison instead, in **one voice for every name** — never the named player's own recording — so that every participant is addressed identically, which is the equal-yet-random property rendered in the acoustic domain as well as the numeric one. Pronunciation authority nonetheless stays with the name's owner in both formats, transferred to a foreign articulator either by modeled repetition (the relay hears the owner's recording immediately before speaking) or by an owner-supplied **respelling** that drives the uniform voice — the pronunciation and the call being two distinct speech acts whose rightful speakers differ.

The sport is parameterized on three orthogonal axes — **method** (the body vocabulary each player declares: hand, paddle, or foot, mixed freely within one circle), **mode** (what the circle plays against: nothing, its own record, or another circle), and **level** (the *lead time* between the call and the object's arrival). The default state has **no score at all**, and its stated purpose is that everyone learns everyone's name with correct pronunciation; at the longest lead time the called player raises a hand, so the ladder from easy to hard is a **scaffold-fading memory curve** rather than a skill ladder — the game becomes more difficult exactly as the group's name recall improves. Scoring degrades gracefully across three tiers — **implied by the call**, **validated by a k-of-N vote of the circle's own microphones**, or **confirmed by an accelerometer in the object** — none of which gates play, and all of which are licensed to be loose because the score moves no value. The system is **local-first**: the entire game runs on one device, offline, with no accounts. **Twenty-three claims** are enumerated and dedicated to the public domain; **eight predictions** are pre-registered, including the design's own existential wager and a test of the address premise itself, both of which the authors commit to publishing either way.

**Keywords:** designed sport, AI officiating, AI-called circulation sport, AI-directed pass calling, deterministic turn assignment, circle game, sey, chinlone, sepak takraw, mixed-age play, handicap systems, loneliness intervention, third place, name learning, cooperative games, defensive publication.

---

## Prior-Art and Non-Assertion Statement

This document and its contents are dedicated to the public domain under the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication. The authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on any mechanism, architecture, or specification articulated herein, in any jurisdiction, at any time.

The following terms are coined in this paper and simultaneously freed with it: **AI-called circulation sport**, **the caller mechanism**, **equal-yet-random distribution**, **the cannot-target-weakness property**, **the dyadic scoring unit**, **start-line handicap** and **quantization-for-dignity**, **the last-gift rule**, **the synced-circle mesh**, and **the play/currency wall**. Freed with the v2 revision: **the call-lead-time ladder**, **scaffold-fading difficulty**, **method-as-declared-handicap**, **the implied point**, **circle-scoped adaptation**, **the acoustic inversion**, **rosterless classroom mode**, and **the sponsorable-place test**. Freed with the 2026-07-27 seat pass: **determined and judged seats**, **the seat-migration bar**, **the determined caller**, **count-only circle coherence**, **the host-agnostic turn-assignment layer**, and **the relay call**. Freed with the present pass: **the address premise**, **the address constraint**, **the uniform calling voice**, **pronunciation-authority transfer**, and **the cross-recording chain**. Terms inherited from this corpus's earlier publications (Proof of Coordinate℠; the mints-nothing boundary; the beating credential) are cited, not re-claimed.

Smart balls, computer-vision officiating, and AI sports-coaching applications are active prior art and an active patent field (§10); the present claims are confined to the *pre-announced named-receiver, equal-random-distribution, dual-arrow, lattice-handicapped circle-sport architecture*, which is, to the authors' knowledge, not previously published as a coherent whole — and to its dignity-preserving constraint set, which is the part an extractive implementation would omit.

---

## 1 · The Premise: A Name, Said by Someone Else

> *"A person's name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language."*
> — Dale Carnegie, *How to Win Friends and Influence People* (1936)

Carnegie offered that as a **technique**. The advice was instrumental — learn names, gain advantage — and the century of sales training built on it has made the sentence faintly embarrassing to quote. This paper keeps the observation and discards the instrumentality. In the sport specified below **nobody chooses whose name is said**, so no participant can deploy a name to their own benefit; the recognition survives and the advantage is engineered out. What remains is the plain finding underneath the salesmanship, which experimental attention research reached independently and from a different direction: a person's own name penetrates a channel they were not attending to, where other words do not (the own-name effect within the cocktail-party phenomenon).

The premise of this sport is one step past that finding, and it is a step Carnegie did not need to take because he was addressing a speaker rather than designing a system.

> **A name spoken aloud is not a sound. It is an *address* — and an address requires someone other than yourself.**

Your own name in your own voice is not an address at all; it is a recording. Nobody is calling you. The sweetness Carnegie describes is not acoustic — it is the evidence a name carries that *another person spent attention on you and kept it*. A remembered name is a receipt for attention already given. This is why being greeted by name by a shopkeeper lands differently from a personalized mail-merge, and why the difference is not one of technology but of **who is doing the addressing**.

From that single premise the sport's architecture follows almost without further argument:

- **Everyone must be addressed, and often.** A game in which some players are called and others are merely present has distributed the sweetest sound unequally, which is what the playground already does. Hence **equal-yet-random** distribution (§4) — equal so that nobody is under-addressed, random so that the address cannot be anticipated and therefore cannot be dismissed.
- **Nobody may choose whom to address.** The instant a participant selects receivers, the address becomes a favor, and a favor withheld is an exclusion. Hence the caller is an **impartial intermediary** and, at §4.2, not even a judgement: an arithmetic that any participant can recompute.
- **The address must not become an evaluation.** A name said because you are good is a rating; a name said because it is your turn is recognition. Hence **no per-player statistics anywhere in the system** (§4.1, §7.1) — the sport that says your name most also refuses to say how you did.
- **The address must be completed.** An address ignored is worse than none. Hence the **dyadic point** (§5): the scoring unit is a call *received*, credited to nobody alone, so the sport's atom is a completed exchange between two people rather than an achievement by one.
- **And no participant may be called in their own voice** (§5.2). This is the premise's hardest and most easily violated consequence, and the one a naive implementation gets wrong: a system holding a recording of each player's name will reach for it at call time, and deliver to each player a recording of themselves. That is not a sport that says your name. It is a mirror.

What the sport produces, then, is not fitness and not a winner. It is a quantity of **addressed attention**, distributed evenly by construction, in a setting where the people doing the addressing are strangers who will now be able to greet each other.

### Why no sport has done this

The premise is not new — every coach who learns thirty names by the second practice is acting on it. What is new is the possibility of *guaranteeing* it, and the guarantee was, until recently, unbuildable. Sport is one of humanity's great social technologies, and like every technology it embodies the constraints of its era. Three of those constraints did most of the shaping, and all three stand between the premise above and any game that could deliver it.

**The officiating constraint.** A fair game needs a neutral judge, and neutral judges are expensive. Most human play therefore proceeds unofficiated — with the familiar result that disputes end games, dominant personalities adjudicate in their own favor, and children learn early that the loudest voice owns the rules. Where officiating exists, it concentrates in a single fallible human who becomes the game's lightning rod: abuse of referees is now so severe that officiating associations in the United States, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere report recruitment collapse, with youth leagues canceled for want of anyone willing to be shouted at. The referee crisis is not a culture problem that better manners will fix; it is a *structure* problem — one human absorbing the full adversarial pressure of everyone else's stakes.

**The matching constraint.** A good game needs opponents of comparable ability, and comparable opponents are rare. Sport's solution was segregation: leagues by age, divisions by skill, categories by sex and weight. The solution works — and quietly forecloses the most valuable game that could exist: the one where a grandmother, a teenager, and a six-year-old contest the same point and all three matter. The family, the one social unit whose play would repair the most, is the unit sport's architecture serves worst. (The lone mainstream counterexample, golf's handicap system, proves the demand: it is the reason golf is one of very few sports a parent and child can genuinely contest, and it required a century of institutional machinery to maintain.)

**The witness constraint.** A game's story needs recording, and recording was expensive, so sport recorded the cheapest summary: *who scored*. From that compression grew the entire statistical culture of sport — batting averages, rankings, ladders, most-valuable-player awards — a fame hierarchy erected on a bookkeeping shortcut. The consequences run downhill to the playground: the child picked last exists because informal sport, too, keeps score of persons; the pickup game has a status economy, and everyone present knows their rank in it.

Machine intelligence ends all three scarcities. Officiating becomes abundant (a phone judges a line call better than a linesman); matching becomes computable (fairness can be *manufactured* rather than found); witness becomes total (everything can be recorded, which forces the question of what *should* be). The default path — already visibly underway in the patent literature (§10) — is to spend this abundance on the old game: more statistics, finer player-surveillance, engagement-optimized training loops. The sport specified below spends it in the opposite direction: on inclusion the matching constraint forbade, on giving the scoring compression erased, and on the one output no sport has ever produced on purpose — *strangers who know each other's names*.

The relation between this section's two halves should be stated exactly, because it is easy to invert. **The address is the premise; the lifted scarcities are the enabling condition.** The abundance did not suggest the goal — a tireless impartial announcer is worth building only if there is a reason every person present should be named aloud, and Carnegie's observation is that reason. What the abundance supplies is the *guarantee*: a circle can now promise every participant an equal share of being addressed, and keep the promise for the whole session, without asking a human to hold the ledger. Everything downstream — the seats, the arithmetic, the two count-arrows, the start-line lattice — exists to protect that guarantee from the ordinary social forces that erode it. A useful test of any proposed change to this specification is therefore not *does it make the game better* but ***does it keep everyone being called by another***.

A design axiom governs throughout, shared by all three papers of this sprint and coined here as **the play/currency wall**: *competition and play may generate the story; only witnessed giving moves the currency.* Winning, in any game this institution builds, may move narrative, honor, or the address of an already-committed gift — never value itself. The wall's application to stakes and patronage is its own paper (*The Wager That Isn't*, this sprint); its application here is simpler and prior: in B-Sey, there is nothing to move. What victory produces is a story.

## 2 · The Canonical Scenes

**A park, late afternoon.** A man finishes a quiet quarter-hour on a bench — the contemplative practice is its own product and no part of this paper — and walks toward a loose ring of people batting a rattan-weight ball into the air. He does not know any of them. Someone widens the circle; he types a name into the app — just *Virak* — and his phone joins the mesh. A moment later every phone in the circle says, in one voice, one word: *"Virak!"* The ball comes to him — gently; the woman who sent it saw a newcomer, and delivery is the whole skill of this game. He gets his paddle under it. The circle cheers the streak alive. Within three rounds, everyone in the circle has heard his name four times, and he has heard all of theirs, because the game cannot proceed without saying them. When the streak dies at 41 — nine short of nothing in particular, since the next rite waits at 333 — the circle groans and laughs, and a stranger says, "Again, Virak?" That sentence — a stranger using his name to invite him back — is the sport's actual product. The rally was the packaging.

**A living room, that evening.** Three generations, one net strung between two chairs. The eight-year-old and her grandmother hold paddles; the parents play with their feet. The family's phones announce in two languages — the grandmother's in Khmer, the child's in English — one circle, one game, two tongues. The teams are uneven, so the app has set the start numbers: the parents begin at 33, the paddle side at 21. First to zero. Nobody chose those numbers; nobody can argue with them; and because the caller decides who receives, the parents cannot serve at the eight-year-old to win — the game has no such move. When the paddle side takes its last point — actively won, as the final point must be — the child performs a victory lap of the sofa. What she has won is the story of having beaten her parents fairly. That is all winning moves here, and it is enough; it has always been enough.

**A classroom, the first week of school.** Thirty children who mostly do not know each other, one teacher who needs to learn thirty names, one ball. The circle solves both problems, because equal-yet-random guarantees every child is called **once the round completes** — and because the round is carried across sessions rather than restarted (§4.3), a class playing ten minutes a day reaches every child instead of cycling the same few. The teacher, standing inside the circle, hears every name spoken aloud dozens of times. No child is picked last, because there is no picking. No child dominates, because the caller will not allow the ball to orbit the confident. The physical-education period and the social-integration project turn out to be the same forty minutes.

## 3 · The Design: One Circle, Five Seats

B-Sey is a circle game for **four or more players in Relay and three or more in Call** (the floor is a function of the format axis; see *Why the floor moves with the format* below), played with a ball designed to be struck by **foot or paddle** — the athletic adult kicks, the grandparent and the child paddle, and both choices are ordinary equipment decisions, not accommodations. Play proceeds in two modes. **Without a net**, the circle plays cooperative keep-alive: the score counts *up*, one per completed reception, and the object is the longest unbroken streak — the collective form. **With a net**, two sides contest a countdown (§5–6) under volleyball-like rally structure — the adversarial form, and the form on which the companion paper's challenge grammar (B-Match℠) nests. A newcomer joins either form the same way: the circle widens. There are no teams to pick in circle mode and no tryout in either; the topology itself is the invitation. **Why the floor moves with the format.** The floor is not a constant but a **function of one variable — whether the caller is a person.** The derivation is single and does not change: **three receivers are required**, because three is the smallest number that leaves any surprise in the call. With two receivers the caller can only alternate — everyone knows who is next before the name is said, and the mechanism this paper specifies contributes nothing.

What changes is only whether a body is spent on calling. **In Relay a human calls and is therefore not receiving, so three receivers cost four players. In Call no human calls, so all present are receivers, and three receivers cost three.** One rule, applied to two arrangements:

```
   required receivers = 3          (invariant — the surprise condition)

   Relay   caller is a person   →  floor = 3 + 1 = 4
   Call    caller is not        →  floor = 3 + 0 = 3
```

⚠️ **This is deliberately *not* a return to the per-mode minimum table withdrawn in v6.** That table restated a number per row, which is exactly how two numbers drift apart. This states the number **once**, as the surprise condition, and lets the format axis supply the only term that varies. The withdrawal stands; what is added is the variable it was missing.

**Provenance, stated asymmetrically because it is asymmetric.** The invariant and its derivation are this paper's own, unchanged since v1. **Three-in-Call is not** — it is prior canon in the product's own design record, where a circle of three standing close with no human caller was specified as the answer for a family of three, and it is the implementation that has been running while this paper said otherwise. The adjacent argument that three is the smallest number at which forward and back differ belongs to the circulation-sport work and is **cited here, not claimed**.

⚠️ **A gap this amendment does not close, and should not be read as closing.** The paper still says nothing about **which formats a Team game may run**, whether a relay caller belongs to a side, or how rotation crosses a net. The floor above is stated for Relay and Call only. Team ships visibly disabled for exactly this reason, and until the axis is specified the honest position is that the format question is open rather than answered by omission.

The machine intelligence in the sport occupies exactly **four seats** — including the one the sport is named for — and is barred from the fifth. The seats fall into two classes, and the division is not a taxonomy for its own sake: it decides how each seat's output can be *checked*, and therefore what an implementer is permitted to put in it.

**The determined seats.** Their output is a pure function of inputs declared before play, so it is checkable by **recomputation** — anyone holding the inputs reproduces the result exactly and sees for themselves that the rule was honoured.

1. **Caller.** The sport's defining mechanism (§4): before each play, the name of the required next receiver, announced aloud. Its selection policy is equal-yet-random and, given the circle and a declared seed, *deterministic* (§4.2) — an arithmetic distribution, not a live opinion about anybody.
2. **Equalizer.** Fairness is manufactured at two points and only two: the **start line** (asymmetric countdown numbers, §6) and the **implement** (paddle or foot, chosen by the player), both drawn from a coarse published lattice. It is never manufactured mid-play. The distinction is load-bearing and stated as a hard rule below.

**The judged seats.** Their output is a perception or a narration. It cannot be reproduced from inputs, so it is checkable only by **explanation** — each judgment stating its ground in one sentence, the standard §5 already imposes on the last-gift ruling.

3. **Umpire.** Line calls, receipt validity, and the classification of the final point (§5) are the system's judgments — instant, neutral, and not attached to a human being who can be shouted at. The referee crisis is answered not by braver referees but by removing the seat the abuse was aimed at.
4. **Witness.** The system records the game's story — the streak, the rally, the celebration — as a *collective* chronicle. It records no player statistics: no individual completion rates, no rankings, no most-valuable anything (§7–8). What it counts, it counts about the circle.

**The barred seat.**

5. **Player — never.** No machine plays. In an age when most activities can be delegated to software, the sport is constructed entirely from the one thing that cannot be: bodies, co-present, attending to each other. The machine is present so that the humans can be.

**The seat-migration bar.** A seat may not take on the other class's mode of operation, and the prohibition runs in both directions because both failures arrive at the same place — a machine-held ranking of persons. A *determined* seat that acquires judgment becomes a rating engine: a caller that routes around a struggling receiver, or a handicapper that tunes start numbers to measured ability, has evaluated the players, and has done it where no one can see it. A *judged* seat that acquires distribution authority becomes a caller: an umpire empowered to influence who receives next can express a preference about people through a channel built for judgments about the ball. The rule is short enough to hold in mind while implementing: **the determined seats never judge a person; the judged seats never choose a person.**

### 3.1 · The three axes: method, mode, level

The sport is parameterized on three orthogonal axes. They are not settings; they are a **ladder**, and an implementation that surfaces them as a configuration screen has already failed the design.

```
   AXIS      QUESTION IT ANSWERS         VALUES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   METHOD    what part of you gives?     hand · paddle · foot
   MODE      what do you play against?   nothing · your record · another circle
   LEVEL     how much warning?           long lead · moderate · short lead
```

**Method** is the body vocabulary a player declares — hand-catch-and-release, paddle, or foot. Anatomy plus implement exhausts the list; there is no fourth. The values are **defaults suggested by ability, never assignments by category**, and heterogeneous methods are expected *within a single circle*: a grandparent with a paddle, a child with hands, an adult with feet, one shared object. This is the load-bearing case, not the exotic one — a sport that segregates by method has thrown away the mixed-age property that is the design's principal social claim, and would have reintroduced by the back door the segregation §1 identifies as sport's inherited disease.

A declared method **is a start-line handicap** (§6) — public, self-chosen, announced before play, never assigned during it — so the axis requires no new fairness machinery; it inherits the machinery already specified. Two consequences follow:

- **The object is constrained by the axis.** One shared object must be catchable, kickable, and paddle-able. A hard ball fails hands; a shuttlecock fails paddle power. A **soft weighted sack** satisfies all three, which is why the reference implementation is a sack rather than a ball.
- **A catch stops flight, so possession needs a bound.** Hand players receive by catching, which would otherwise let a player hold the object and stall the circle. The rule: **catch and release within one beat, where the caller's own cadence is the release clock.** As lead time shortens (§4.1) the hand method converts from catch-and-throw to volley-tap without a rule change — difficulty emerges from the method mixture rather than being imposed on it.

**Mode** is what the circle plays against, and the values ascend: *nothing* (**Friendship**, no scoring of any kind), *its own record* (**Streak**, no net, ascending collective count), *another circle* (**Team**, net, descending count to zero, and the only mode additionally requiring enough players to form two sides). All three take their floor from the single rule of §3 — **three receivers, plus a body for the caller only where the caller is a person** (Relay 4, Call 3). The per-mode minimum *table* given in revisions before v6 remains withdrawn and is not restored: it restated a number per row, which is how two numbers drift apart. One number, stated once, with one variable. The mode names are deliberate: **no label on the product surface names rivalry**, though the adversarial mode is genuinely adversarial and this paper describes it as such. Naming the third mode for its structural novelty — *sides exist* — rather than for its disposition is a small instance of a general discipline in this corpus, in which vocabulary is held to the same standard as mechanism.

The mode ladder is also the **adoption funnel**, and an unusually honest one: each rung is entered by the circle's own election, each rung's graduation is the previous rung's success condition, and the entry rung has **no score at all**.

**Level** is treated in §4.1, because it is a property of the caller rather than of the players.

**The three-value pattern is not aesthetic and should not be read as one.** Each axis has an independent reason for its cardinality: method is exhausted by anatomy plus implement; mode is exhausted by the opponent relation; level is coarsely quantized for the same anti-rating reason the start-line lattice is (§6) — a continuously variable difficulty dial would read as a precision skill rating, which is the artifact this design exists to avoid. Where a fourth value would genuinely serve — very large circles may want a fourth lead-time band — the pattern must yield. **Three is a finding here, not a constraint.**

## 4 · The Caller: Equal-Yet-Random, and the Property It Buys

The sport's one genuinely novel mechanism is small enough to state in a sentence: **before each strike, the system announces by name the player who must receive next.**

Everything distinctive about B-Sey follows from that sentence.

**Equal-yet-random distribution.** The caller's selection policy has two commitments that are individually trivial and jointly unprecedented in sport. *Equal*: **over a complete round** — one pass through the roster — every player in the circle receives the same number of touches, within rounding, and the weakest player is guaranteed the strongest player's share of the game. **Revisions of this paper before v6 stated this over a *session*, and that overstated it**: a session is a prefix of a round, and a prefix of a fair sequence is not fair. The guarantee is reachable under real usage only because rounds are carried across sessions rather than restarted (§4.3). *Random*: the order is unpredictable, so no player can disengage — anyone's name may be next, and the suspense that in ordinary sport attaches only to the ball here attaches to every person simultaneously. Equality without randomness would be a queue (predictable, boring, and stigmatizing — everyone can see whose turn is being "given"); randomness without equality is every pickup game ever played (the ball orbits the skilled). The conjunction is the mechanism.

**The cannot-target-weakness property.** In net mode, the caller designates receivers on *both* sides. The attacking side therefore cannot choose to serve at the weakest opponent — the oldest strategy in net sports, taught openly at every level, and the precise mechanism by which the weakest player on any volleyball court spends the match being hunted. In B-Sey that strategy does not exist. It is not penalized; it is not discouraged; it is *absent from the move-set*, the way castling into check is absent from chess. Skill, denied the target-selection channel, migrates entirely into **delivery** — placing the ball so your designated receiver, whoever the caller named, can continue the play. The best player in a B-Sey circle is definitionally the one who makes everyone else look good, because making the named receiver succeed is the only thing the rules allow skill to do. To the authors' knowledge, no prior net sport has this property, and it is claimed here as the design's sharpest single contribution (Claim 2).

**The name as by-product and as point.** Because the call is a *name*, spoken aloud, repeatedly, by every device in the circle (§7), the sport performs introductions as a side effect of its basic loop. This is not a social feature bolted onto a game; it is the game's addressing layer, doing double duty. The design intends the double duty (§9's first prediction measures it): B-Sey is built to be the first sport whose standard output includes *strangers who know each other's names* — the missing primitive of the third place.

**Hard constraints on the caller** (stated here as design law; their governance form lives in the institution's internal directive registry):

- The caller **never evaluates players in the flow of play**. It does not skew calls by skill, win probability, or match situation; it does not route around a struggling receiver at a tense moment. A caller that "protects" the weak player at match point has rebuilt picked-last-at-recess inside an algorithm, invisibly, which is worse than the playground original because it cannot be seen and argued with. Fairness lives at the start line only.
- The caller speaks **chosen names only** — the name a player registers for the circle, which may be a nickname; children's circles use first names or nicknames as a rule. No legal name is ever broadcast across a public park.
- Per-player data that the equalizer uses (implement choice, start-number calibration) is a **private mirror** — visible to the player, never to the circle, never to any ranking, never retained as a skill profile.

### 4.1 · Level as call lead time: a scaffold-fading memory curve

The naive difficulty dial for a called sport is the interval between calls. It is the wrong variable: the inter-call interval is confounded by circle size, so the same setting produces a frantic game with four players and a languid one with thirty. The correct variable is **call lead time** — the interval between the naming of the receiver and the object's arrival. Lead time is invariant to circle size and to method, and it is what a receiver actually experiences as pressure.

Three bands are specified, and what changes across them is not merely speed but **how much external scaffolding supports the act of recognition**:

```
   LEVEL     LEAD TIME    SCAFFOLD                    WHAT IS BEING TRAINED
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Easy      long         called player RAISES A HAND  nothing yet — the
                          and may speak their own      circle is being taught
                          name aloud                   the names
   Medium    moderate     none — the giver must find   name → face recall
                          the named face unaided
   Hard      short        none; the call may land      automaticity under
                          while the object is aloft    time pressure
```

At the longest lead the called player **raises a hand**, which removes the recall requirement entirely: a giver who does not yet know who *Sokha* is can simply deliver to the raised hand. The scaffold is then withdrawn — first the hand, then the time — and the withdrawal is enforced by physics rather than by rule, since a hand cannot usefully be raised inside a short lead.

The result is that **the difficulty ladder is a memory curve, not a skill curve.** A circle can only ascend it as its members' name recall becomes fast and then automatic, which yields the design's cleanest coincidence: *the game becomes more fun exactly as everyone learns each other's names.* The thing the players want and the thing the sport is for are the same thing, and no exhortation is required to align them.

It also supplies the sport's non-numeric progression. In Friendship mode there is no score, and the circle nonetheless has something that advances: **tempo is the score that is not a score.**

**A constraint the implementer must not violate.** It is tempting to advance the level automatically from measured response latency. Doing so *per player* would reconstruct, invisibly and in the tempo dimension, precisely the artifact §4 exists to prevent — a machine-maintained ranking of who is slow. The rule:

> **The level is a property of the circle, never of a player.**

Permitted implementations, in order of preference: (a) **the circle elects the level**, with the caller permitted to *offer* an advance; (b) if adaptive at all, adaptation conditions **only on circle-aggregate state**, ephemeral and on-device, never per-player, never stored, never displayed. Never permitted: a per-player recall score, in any form, visible or not.

### 4.2 · The determined caller: fairness as arithmetic

The caller is the seat where an implementer will most want to put intelligence, and the seat where intelligence does the most damage. This design resolves the tension by removing the caller from the domain of judgment altogether: **the call sequence is a deterministic pure function of the circle's roster and a seed declared before play.** Given the same roster and seed, every conforming implementation emits a bit-identical sequence, which makes the generator a cross-platform contract rather than an internal detail.

Three properties follow. The third was not anticipated when the constraint was adopted, and is now the reason to keep it.

**Fairness becomes verifiable rather than trusted.** Equal-yet-random (§4) is the sport's central promise and the one a participant is least able to check by watching, since over any short window a fair sequence and a biased one look alike — which is precisely why a sport that merely *asserts* fair distribution asks to be taken at its word. When the roster and seed are the entire input, any participant, parent, teacher, or competitor can recompute a completed session and confirm that the distribution was equal and that no one was skipped, favoured, or quietly protected. Publishing the generator is therefore part of the mechanism rather than a disclosure concession.

**Multi-device play stops requiring a network.** Because each device computes the sequence independently, devices in one circle need never be told *who* is next — only **how many calls have elapsed**. A single integer, not a name, is the whole synchronization payload; a device rejoining after a lapse fast-forwards to the current index instead of recovering state. Where simultaneous announcement (§7) demands tight clock alignment, sequence *agreement* demands none at all. The offline-first commitment of §7.1 is thus not merely compatible with the determined caller — it is largely delivered by it.

**There is no per-player state to leak, subpoena, or repurpose.** The forbidden artifact of §4 and §4.1 — a machine-maintained record of who is slow, who is skipped, who is protected — is not merely prohibited here by policy. A pure function of a roster and a seed has nowhere to keep such a record. The guarantee moves out of the governance layer and into the arithmetic, where a later release cannot quietly relax it and an acquirer cannot monetize it.

**The general lesson, offered to implementers of any called game.** A fairness property enforced by a rule *about* the algorithm lasts exactly as long as the organization enforcing it; the same property enforced by determinism and published vectors outlasts the organization. Where a guarantee can be made checkable, making it checkable is worth more than making the underlying decision cleverer — and the two are usually opposed, because the intelligence that would improve a decision is the same thing that makes it unauditable.

None of this disarms the machine; it relocates it. Perception and narration — was the ball in, was the final point actively won, what is this circle's story — are irreducibly judgments, and they are where sensing and inference legitimately belong. The boundary is worth restating at the hardware layer beside the warning already given there (§7.1): **instrumentation serves the judged seats only.** An accelerometer reporting a touch supplies the umpire with evidence. It must never supply the caller with a reason.


### 4.3 · Round continuity: the unit is the round, not the session

The equal-distribution guarantee holds over a **complete round** — one pass through the roster — and not over an arbitrary slice of one. The distinction is not pedantry. It is the difference between a working guarantee and a broken one, and the reference implementation shipped the broken version first.

A class of thirty playing a ten-minute warm-up calls perhaps ten children. If the caller's progress resets when the session ends, the next session calls the same ten, and the twenty children at the far end of the round are never called at all — every day, indefinitely, with nothing on any surface to indicate it. The distribution is perfectly equal within each session and catastrophically unequal across them. **An invariant enforced only within a unit is silently void across units, and the unit boundary is where nobody looks.**

The repair is to persist the round rather than the session. The caller retains a **circle-scoped integer call index** — never a per-participant record, never a timestamp — so that a truncated session resumes where it stopped rather than restarting: whoever has not been called yet is still uncalled tomorrow. This is what makes the guarantee reachable under real usage, in which play is chopped into ten-minute pieces by bells, weather, and attention.

Two properties are worth stating for implementers. First, the persisted state is **a single integer per circle**, which is why it introduces no per-participant artifact and nothing to leak (§4.2). Second, **no amount of session-level testing detects the defect**, because every test anyone would write runs one session, and within one session the distribution is exactly correct. A competitor implementing from this specification would ship the same bug.

## 5 · Scoring: The Dyadic Point and the Two Arrows

**The dyadic scoring unit.** A point increments when the *named receiver successfully receives*. The unit of scoring is therefore not a strike, a kill, or a goal — acts one player performs — but a completed **give-and-receive**: a delivery good enough to be received, and a reception good enough to continue. Nobody scores alone, structurally. The compression error of historical scorekeeping (§1) — recording the last touch and calling it the achievement — is not corrected by tracking assists (a patch several sports have tried) but by defining the point as the *pair*. In the institutional grammar this corpus builds elsewhere, the point is a witnessed micro-gift; within this paper it is enough that it is a *dyad*, and that the sport's atomic event requires two people succeeding together.

**Count up (the circle).** Cooperative keep-alive counts consecutive completed receptions. The streak is a built thing — collective, cumulative, mortal. When it dies, it dies for everyone at once, and the circle starts again: the game's only loss condition is shared by all players equally, which is why circle-mode B-Sey has no losers at all, only a streak that was and the next one. Streak milestones are celebrated at the **repdigits** — 3, 33, 333, 3333 — an exponential rationing that keeps each rite roughly ten times rarer than the last (a celebration every 33 would inflate to wallpaper across a long streak; a celebration at repdigits stays an event for the rest of the sport's life). Between rites, the circle's *record* — the park record, the school record — carries continuous motivation. Records belong to circles and places, never to persons.

**Count down (the net).** Adversarial B-Sey inverts the scoreboard: each side begins at a start number (§6) and every rally won *subtracts* one from the winner's remaining count. **First to zero wins** — first to nothing. The arithmetic is identical to counting up; the symbolism is its inversion, and a scoreboard is nothing but symbolism: the winning team is the team that first gives away everything it started with. Rally structure follows volleyball (serve rotation; a point every rally). Two refinements complete the mode:

- **The last-gift rule.** A side's final point — the one from 1 to 0 — must be *actively won*: earned by that side's successful play, never conferred by an opponent's unforced error. No match may end on a serve into the net; the anticlimax that deflates conventional rally scoring at its most important moment is ruled out. (Darts' double-out finish is the honest precedent: the insight that endings must be earned is old; its application to rally sport is claimed here.) Classification of a final rally as actively-won is the umpire seat's call, held to the same one-sentence-explainability as every other judgment in the system.
- **No deuce.** Conventional win-by-two exists to prevent flukish endings between equal teams; B-Sey's endings are already guarded by the last-gift rule, and its equality is already engineered at the start line. Adding deuce on top would re-lengthen games unpredictably and dilute the countdown's clean terminus at zero.

**Both arrows, one ruleset.** Cooperative sports count up; adversarial sports count up; darts and little else count down. A single sport in which the *mode selects the arrow* — building in the circle, emptying at the net — is, to the authors' knowledge, novel, and is claimed as architecture (Claim 5): the two arrows are not a gimmick but the two halves of the institution's founding game (a children's balance game in which kindness counts up and gratitude counts down and the ideal score is zero), expressed as sport.

**What the arrows do is move the opponent.** In an ordinary net sport the opponent is a person, and every point is taken from someone. The arrows relocate that. Counting up, the circle plays against **the drop** — gravity, entropy, its own prior record. Counting down, it plays against another circle, by agreement. A third position exists and is the one the level ladder of §4.1 occupies: the opponent as **the circle's own earlier state**, which is competition that costs no one anything. This is why the entry rung carries no score at all and why advancement between modes is elected rather than triggered (§3.1). The sport does not remove competition; it makes the choice of opponent explicit and puts the adversarial option last.

### 5.1 · The scoring ladder, and the implied point

Scoring in a called sport admits an architecture unavailable to every other game, and it follows from one observation: **the caller has already assigned identity.** Every other sport must determine *who* touched the object; this one *chose* who touches it next. What remains to be established is only whether the touch occurred — a binary event, not a localization problem.

Three tiers implement that, and each degrades gracefully into the one below:

```
   TIER       MECHANISM                                    HARDWARE
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   default    the point is IMPLIED by the call —           none
              assume the dyad completed
   validated  k-of-N vote across the circle's own          none
              phone microphones: "was there a strike
              in this window?"
   confirmed  accelerometer in the object reports          instrumented
              {object_id, touch, t}                        object
```

**Sensing never gates play.** A circle with one phone and a rolled sock plays the whole sport; instrumentation improves fidelity and nothing else.

The **microphone tier** deserves note because it is cheap for a non-obvious reason. Localizing a strike acoustically across phones — time-difference-of-arrival — is a research problem: it needs tight clock synchronization and degrades badly in wind and traffic. **Detecting** one does not. A strike is a sharp transient, separable from ambient noise on a single microphone; a **k-of-N agreement rule** across the circle tolerates a phone in a pocket, a gust, and a passing motorcycle; and the vote requires only a coarse shared window, which the mesh's announcement synchronization (§7) already supplies. The reduction from localization to detection is what moves this tier from research to implementation, and it is available *only* because the caller supplies identity.

**The implied point is an epistemic claim, not a semantic one — and the distinction is load-bearing.** The scoring unit remains what §5 defines: a completed delivery-and-reception pair, credited to no individual. The default tier does not redefine the point; it **assumes the dyad completed and permits a human, or later a sensor, to say otherwise.** An implementation that treated the *call itself* as the scoring event would have quietly built a different game — one in which the caller scores — and would have destroyed the dyadic unit that §5 claims. The caller never scores.

**Why such loose epistemics are licensed here.** Because of §8: no point mints, moves, or gates value. **A score that moves nothing requires no audit.** Were the score coupled to money, the instrumented tier would be mandatory and the default tier negligent; because it is not, trust is the correct default and sensing is an amenity. This is a case of a constraint adopted for dignity reasons removing an engineering dependency — the play/currency wall paying for itself in hardware.

One consequence for the record architecture (§12, claim 10): a trusted-by-default streak can silently inflate. **Records therefore carry their evidence tier** — *unvalidated*, *microphone-validated*, or *object-confirmed* — so that a circle's record states not only its magnitude but how it was witnessed.

### 5.2 · The three speaker formats, and the acoustic inversion

A circle has **one acoustic channel and two candidates for it**: the name of the next receiver, and the count. They cannot both be the headline. Interleaving them — *"Sokha! … fourteen! … Dara! … fifteen!"* — buries the name in numerals, and the name is what the sport is for.

The specification therefore inverts the convention of every scoring sport in existence:

> **Every other scoring sport calls the score. This one calls the person.**

The formats below are **named rather than numbered**, deliberately: one constraint stated at the end of this section must survive any future reordering of the list, and a rule that says *"format 1"* breaks the moment a format is inserted ahead of it.

**Relay (the default, and the format a first deployment should ship).** The system speaks the name **privately to a single human relay** — through that person's own device, audibly to them alone — and that person calls it aloud to the circle. Selection remains machine-held, so every distribution property of §4 survives intact; what changes is only who moves the air. The consequences are larger than the modification: there is **no loudspeaker, no mesh, no clock alignment, and no requirement that participants own devices**, so a single borrowed handset serves an entire circle. That matters most exactly where the sport is most wanted — a school that prohibits phones, a park with no signal, a group in which one person has a device.

Two further properties were not the reason for the arrangement and are now the reason to keep it. First, the relay **hears the participant-approved pronunciation immediately before producing it**, which makes correct articulation a *modeled repetition* rather than a reading task; a name read off a screen is mangled precisely for the names this design exists to protect. Second, and more consequential: **the relay produces names aloud, where a player only ever hears them.** The role is therefore where the sport's stated purpose is actually practised, and it follows that the role must **rotate under the same equal-yet-random assignment that distributes receptions**. Left to the circle, the confident participant holds the device and the quiet one never says a name — picked-last rebuilt through the back door of the very role meant to distribute the practice. Rotation also disposes of the objection that the relay is excluded from play: the role is a turn, not a sacrifice. The honest cost is a **tempo ceiling** — the repeat beat is absorbed at long lead times and binds at short ones — which is what the synchronized mesh (§7) is *for*, as a later upgrade rather than a launch prerequisite.

**Call — the name format, spoken to the circle.** The system addresses the whole circle directly over the mesh in **one voice for every name** — never in the named participant's own recorded voice, for the reason given at the end of this section — and **counts silently.** The count is *visible, not audible*: the mesh already places a screen in every pocket, and adversarial mode's countdown must remain readable for tension and tactics. Silence is not concealment. Numbers are spoken only at the rationed celebration thresholds of §6, which means **a spoken number is always a rite** rather than ambient noise. The chant, if the circle wants one, remains entirely human — the system never leads it and never competes with it. *An accessibility setting must permit a spoken count, off by default, for players who cannot read the screen; the pre-announcement of §4 is already an auditory pre-cue and the same constituency is served by both.*

**Free — the count format, with the caller off.** The caller is disabled entirely; the system counts aloud *with* the circle, and nobody is told where to pass. This is free play with a shared, trusted counter — and it exists because the design's central mechanism is unproven (§9, §11). It is also **why the microphone tier is specified**: with no call, the system has nothing to count from unless it *hears* the strike. The two are one feature.

The formats are **mutually exclusive by construction** — a session runs exactly one — which resolves the apparent contradiction among them. The rule was never that numbers are undesirable; it is that **the name must never compete with numerals** — one voice per channel, and the channel's content follows what the mode is for.

### 5.3 · The address constraint: no one is called in their own voice

Across every format, one constraint governs *articulation* rather than selection, and it follows directly from §1:

> **The voice that says a participant's name must never be that participant's own.**

The constraint has to be stated because the obvious implementation violates it. A system that teaches correct pronunciation will hold a recording of each name made by its owner — that is the only honest source of the pronunciation — and at call time the nearest artifact to hand is exactly that recording. Playing it delivers to each participant a recording of themselves saying their own name. The result is not a poor address; it is **not an address at all**, and no amount of audio quality repairs it.

Naming the constraint separates two speech acts that a single artifact had been performing at once, and which have different rightful speakers:

| | **The pronunciation** | **The call** |
|---|---|---|
| Whose is it? | the name's owner | anyone but the owner |
| What is it for? | how the name sounds | *you, now* |
| Failure mode | anglicization | self-address; no speaker |
| Where it lives | a stored model, approved by its owner | the moment of play |

The two are joined by **transfer**, not by identity: the owner's authority over how the name sounds is carried *into a voice that is not theirs*. Two mechanisms accomplish this, one per format. In **Relay**, the human caller hears the owner's own recording immediately before speaking, and reproduces it — modeled repetition, the highest-fidelity transfer available, and the reason the default format is also the best one. In **Call**, where every participant is a player and no human other is free to speak, the owner supplies a **respelling** — the name written as it sounds — which the single system voice articulates. The respelling is not an accessibility fallback; it is the transfer mechanism itself, and the only route by which a participant's authority over their own name reaches a synthetic articulator.

**One voice for every name is a property, not a limitation.** A circle whose calls were assembled from twelve different recordings would address each participant in a different timbre — the texture of being called would vary by whose recording happened to be playing. A single voice calling everyone means **every participant is addressed identically**: equal-yet-random rendered in sound. The uniformity of the acoustic channel is the audible form of the fairness the caller already guarantees numerically.

A note on what this does *not* claim. A system voice is an *other*, which is what the premise strictly requires, but it is not a *person*, and §1's account of why a name is sweet — evidence that someone spent attention on you — is only partly satisfied by a machine. This is a real gap and the specification does not paper over it: it is the reason **Relay is the default format and Call is the device-plentiful case**, rather than the reverse. Where a human can say your name, one should.

#### The circle's own voices: cross-recorded calls

The gap above admits a partial repair, specified here as an **option within Call** rather than as a fourth format, because it changes which audio plays and not what anyone does during a rally.

The intuition is that a circle calling itself in its own members' voices would be warmer than a circle called by one synthetic voice, and it is correct. The naive implementation of it is nonetheless barred by the constraint above: playing each participant the recording *they themselves made* is precisely the mirror this section exists to prevent, and the warmth is illusory because the one voice a participant never hears as an address is their own. **The intuition survives; the implementation must be inverted.**

**The mechanism is a cross-recording chain.** At join, after a participant records their own name — the pronunciation model, which stays theirs — the device passes to the next participant, who is shown that name, hears the model, and **says it themselves**. That second recording is the *call* audio. The device continues around the circle, so each participant records exactly one other participant's name and is recorded by exactly one other participant: a cyclic permutation of the roster, costing one additional beat of roughly three seconds per person and producing exactly *N* artifacts rather than *N²*.

Four properties follow, none of which the uniform voice provides:

1. **Every call is a human voice, and never the listener's own** — the address constraint is satisfied in its strong form rather than its formal one, because the speaker is a person who spent attention on the listener.
2. **The distribution is exactly even by construction**, as the caller's is: one recording made by each participant, one recording naming each participant. The property that governs receptions governs voices.
3. **It runs the production effect at join**, before play begins. The rotating relay role teaches participants to *produce* names rather than merely hear them (§5.2); the chain does the same thing one beat earlier and for every participant at once, including in Call, where no relay role exists to do it.
4. **The recording is itself a small gift** — a participant spends three seconds so that another can be called — which is the sport's own subject enacted before the first rally.

The owner's approval (§5.3, and claim 21) governs the call audio as it governs every other pronunciation artifact: a chain recording a participant has not approved does not enter play, and the participant may ask for another take without stating a reason.

**When to offer it, and when not.** The two voicings answer different circles and the specification declines to rank them absolutely. Among **strangers**, the uniform voice is the better default: an identical acoustic channel is itself a fairness signal, and a newcomer has no relationship to the voice that would say their name — a stranger's recording of it carries no more warmth than a machine's while carrying more opportunity for mockery. Among people who **already know each other** — a family, a classroom after its first week, a returning circle — the chain is better, because the voices mean something and the sport's remaining work is warmth rather than fairness. The honest cost is stated plainly: **the chain forfeits the addressed-identically property**, and a circle that adopts it has traded a fairness signal for a warmth signal, which is a reasonable trade only once fairness is no longer the live question.

Two failure modes and their handling. A participant who leaves mid-session takes their recording's referent with them but not their recorded voice; a participant joining late has no one in the chain. In both cases the affected name **falls back to the uniform voice for the remainder of the session** rather than to the participant's own recording — the constraint holds under degradation, which is where constraints are actually tested.

**Three constraints on Free, because it switches the sport's dignity guarantees off.** Equal-touch distribution and the cannot-target-weakness property both live *in the caller*; with the caller off, humans choose receivers again and the picked-last dynamic returns. Accordingly: **(a)** a caller-on format remains the default everywhere; **(b)** Free must never be represented to an institution as equivalent — the anti-exclusion properties an administrator approves are precisely the caller's, and a free-play session does not carry them; **(c)** **any trial of the caller mechanism must run a caller-on format** — Relay or Call — or it measures nothing. That constraint is stated by *property* rather than by position in this list, which is why the formats carry names: a future revision may add or reorder formats, and the rule must not silently come to designate the wrong one. On which point see §9.1: Free is not merely a fallback but the natural **control arm** for the experiment that tests the caller itself.
