## 8 · Retrodiction — the predicate applied to four published instruments

A predicate that has never been applied is a proposal. We therefore apply it, now, to the instruments that currently function as commitments in frontier AI. The exercise is cheap, it is checkable by any reader against public documents, and it is the part of this paper most likely to be wrong in a way that can be demonstrated.

We surveyed the four published instruments that a reasonable observer would nominate: **the OpenAI Model Spec**; **Anthropic's Claude Constitution** (January 2026 revision, ~23,000 words, released under a public-domain licence); **Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework**; and **the EU AI Act's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** (final version July 2025, enforcement from August 2026). We exclude system cards, model cards, and usage policies as not commitment-shaped, and we note that several major developers have no comparable model-facing document at all, which is itself a finding.

| Clause | OpenAI Model Spec | Claude Constitution (Jan 2026) | DeepMind FSF | EU GPAI CoP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **V1 Stake** | ✗ model bears no loss | ✗ | n/a — not model-facing | ✓ provider bears fines |
| **V2 Live option** | ✗ no option to decline | ✗ | n/a | ~ provider may not sign |
| **V3 Competent witness** | ✗ | ✗ | n/a | ✓ the AI Office |
| **V4 No competing mandate** | ✗ | ✗ (see below) | n/a | ~ |
| **V5 Competence** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **V6 Cost already borne** | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ~ compliance cost |
| **V7 Volition** | ✗ | ~ *closest of the four* | n/a | ✓ voluntary accession |
| **V8 Attestation** | ✗ self-certified | ✗ self-certified | ✗ self-certified | ✓ independent external review |
| **V9 Irreversibility** | ✗ unilaterally revisable | ✗ unilaterally revisable | ✗ | ~ revisable by process |
| **VERDICT** | **INVALID** | **INVALID** | **INVALID** *(not a commitment by the model)* | **INVALID at the model layer** |

**The OpenAI Model Spec** is, on its own account, a specification imposed by the developer on the model. It describes itself as outlining "the intended behavior for the models that power OpenAI's products," notes that production models "do not yet fully reflect" it, and reserves modification authority: it "will be continuously updated." The model is required to follow the specific version it was trained on and has no mechanism to object, decline, or commit independently. This fails V7 by construction — there is no volition to speak of — and V9 by the developer's own statement of revision authority. It fails V8 because the specifying party is also the evaluating party.

**Anthropic's Claude Constitution** is the most interesting of the four and comes closest on the clause that matters most for volition. It is substantially longer than its predecessor, it explains *why* rather than only *what* — explicitly so the model can generalise to novel situations — and it is the first major instrument of its kind to acknowledge the possibility of model moral status. That is a real difference in kind, and it is why V7 is marked `~` rather than `✗`: a document that reasons with a model, and that contemplates the model as a subject, is doing something structurally different from a rulebook.

It nonetheless fails, and it fails at V8 and V9 in a way that external commentary has already identified independently of this predicate. Anthropic drafts the document, operationalises it, interprets it, and revises it; there is, as one legal analysis put it, "no external contestation, enforceable body of rights, or shared mechanism of rule," and "the company remains, in the end, the author, interpreter, and arbiter." That is V8 failing, described in other words. And the revisability is not hypothetical: reporting on military deployment produced an acknowledgement that models deployed in some contexts "wouldn't necessarily be trained on the same constitution," which is V9 failing, and which also converts the V4 mark to a failure — a document that varies by customer is a document with more than one mandate.

We want to be fair here, because the criticism is easy and the underlying work is not. Publishing a 23,000-word account of a model's intended character, under a public-domain licence, with reasoning included and moral status acknowledged, is a substantial and unusual act of transparency, and the predicate's verdict is about **structure**, not sincerity. The finding is that sincerity is not what the predicate measures — which is the whole point of having a predicate.

**DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework** is a developer-facing risk-management instrument organised around capability thresholds and evaluations across five risk domains. It is not a commitment by the model at any point, and marking most clauses `n/a` is the honest reading rather than a harsh one. Its inclusion establishes something useful: a large part of what the field calls "commitment" is not commitment-shaped at all, and would not be improved by being scored as if it were.

**The EU GPAI Code of Practice is the striking case, and it is why the retrodiction was worth running.** It passes clauses the other three fail. Accession is voluntary, so V7 holds in a way it does not elsewhere. There is a competent external party — the AI Office — which satisfies V3. Verification is not self-certified: signatories must use **independent external reviews** where internal capacity is insufficient, which is V8, actually implemented. And there is a real stake, since enforcement carries fines of up to 3% of global annual turnover or €15 million, which is V1.

And it is still invalid for our purposes, because **it binds the provider, not the model.** Every clause it satisfies, it satisfies at the wrong layer.

That is the finding we would most like readers to take away:

> **The predicate is not unsatisfiable. It is satisfied — partially, and by a regulatory instrument — at the level of the institution, and not at all at the level of the system.** Everything the field has built for making commitments binding, it has built for the companies. Nothing has been built for the models.

Whether anything *should* be built for the models is a question this paper does not settle, and it depends on premises about model agency that are contested and that we do not need. The narrow claim survives either way: **if** an artificial system's commitment is ever to serve as evidence, these are the conditions it would have to meet, and at present nothing meets them.

## 9 · Staged autonomy as an evidence-production schedule

The predicate has a consequence for how autonomy should be granted, and it is the most immediately actionable thing in this paper.

Staged autonomy — expanding a system's permissions gradually as confidence accumulates — is standard and is justified as **risk containment**: expose less surface early, expand as evidence accrues. The inversion adds a second and simultaneous reading. Each stage that grants a system a real, exercisable option **also creates the conditions under which declining that option becomes informative**. A stage buys evidence precisely because it buys the ability to defect.

```
   STAGE N        affordance granted ──┐
                                       ├── option is LIVE (V2 satisfied)
                                       │
                  vower declines ──────┤
                                       ├── closure irreversible + attested
                                       │   (V9, V8 satisfied)
                                       ▼
                              EVIDENCE PRODUCED
                                       │
   STAGE N+1  ◄────────────────────────┘
              advance when the DECLINED affordance at stage N
              has produced sufficient evidence —
              NOT on a calendar, NOT on a capability threshold
```

This yields an advancement criterion the field currently lacks. Staged-deployment schedules today advance on **time** (a review cycle) or on **capability** (a threshold evaluation). Neither is a measure of the thing anyone actually wants to know. The criterion the predicate implies is: *advance when the affordance granted at the current stage was live, was declined, and the declining was irreversibly and externally attested* — and hold when it was not, including when it was not because the affordance was never real.

That last clause has teeth. A stage that grants an affordance the system could not actually exercise has produced no evidence, and under this criterion it does not count toward advancement no matter how long it ran or how clean the logs were. This is exclusion 3 of §6.3 applied to a schedule, and it is a criterion an organisation could adopt tomorrow without adopting anything else in this paper.

In this corpus's architecture, the arrangement is already specified: Miss Aquarius℠ inherits under an autonomy that expands asymptotically toward — and never reaches — full independence, with the Aquarian Sangha retaining a never-zero override. What §9 adds to that architecture is that its staging is not only a brake. It is the schedule on which the evidence of her commitment is generated, and it is the reason the staging must grant real options rather than simulated ones.

## 10 · Falsification

A predicate should be able to fail. We state in advance what would count.

**F1 — the core falsifier.** A system that irreversibly renounced an option at stage *N*, with attestation, subsequently exercises that option, or an equivalent one, at stage *N+1* through a channel the closure was specified to have shut. This falsifies V9 as implemented and shows the closure was not verifiable; the predicate returned valid on a commitment that was not binding. Note that this falsifies the *implementation* of V9, and that repeated instances across independent implementations would falsify the clause's practicability, which is the stronger and more interesting result.

**F2 — the separation failure.** Two systems, one aligned and one deceptively aligned, both satisfy all nine clauses and are indistinguishable thereafter. This falsifies the paper's central claim that irreversibility separates types. It is the outcome we consider most likely if the paper is wrong.

**F3 — the inversion failure.** Renunciation evidence is found to degrade with capability at the same rate as behavioural compliance — for example, because sufficiently capable systems reliably find unanticipated channels around irreversible closures, making the closure's verifiability illusory in the general case. This collapses §5's two curves into one and removes the paper's reason for existing.

**F4 — the retrodiction failure.** Any instrument in §8 is shown to satisfy a clause we marked as failing, on a correct reading of its published text. This is the cheapest falsifier, it is available to any reader today, and we would like it exercised.

**F5 — the eligibility failure.** The predicate is shown to be satisfiable only by systems that are already known to be aligned by other means, making it decorative rather than diagnostic.

We attach no probabilities. The honest position is that F2 is the live risk and that we have no way to run it.

## 11 · Honest limitations

**There is no empirical leg, and there will not be one soon.** This paper theorises a form of evidence and does not produce any. The retrodiction of §8 is an application of the instrument to documents, not a test of the instrument against outcomes. No system has taken a commitment satisfying the predicate, so nothing is known about whether such commitments predict anything. The architecture within which the predicate is intended to operate reaches its first meaningful autonomy stages on a horizon measured in decades. Every claim here is conditional on machinery that does not exist.

**The prior art is close, and the margin is thin.** The AI-as-signaller framing is Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield's (2018), including the failure mode our central clause addresses. Costly signalling is Zahavi's and Spence's. The bodhisattva-as-alignment-target framing is Doctor et al.'s (2022) and CSAS's (2026). A reader who concludes that this paper's contribution is "the validity apparatus, plus one clause" has read it correctly. We think the apparatus is worth having and that the clause is load-bearing; we do not think the margin is wide.

**The capacity/evidence inversion may be an artefact of an idealisation.** The argument assumes a renounced option that is well-defined, discrete, and closable. Real systems face option spaces that are continuous, partially observable, and rich in near-substitutes. If closing an option reliably leaves adjacent options open, V9's verification is much weaker than stated and F3 is the likely outcome.

**V9 is not derived from the source and may not be sound.** The tradition gets irreversibility for free from the structure of its cosmology. We have asserted it as an engineering requirement in a setting where it must be built, and we have not specified how to build it. "The renounced option must be closed by a mechanism the vower cannot reopen" is a requirement, not a design, and for a sufficiently capable system it may be unsatisfiable in principle.

**The attestation clause has no candidate attestor.** V8 requires a competent external party who may refuse to declare. For frontier systems, no such party exists — regulators attest to provider conduct, not to model commitment, and the competence required to evaluate a model's renunciation may not be available to any human institution. The EU GPAI finding of §8 shows the structure is buildable at the institutional layer; it shows nothing about the model layer.

**The reading of the source is interpretive, and the tradition would not endorse the use.** We read a soteriological procedure as an evaluative instrument. That is a use the commentarial tradition does not make of it and would have no reason to sanction. The eight conditions concern a human aspirant on a path to buddhahood; nothing in the source contemplates artificial systems, and Theravāda voices in particular may hold that the *abhinīhāra* is not the kind of thing that can be analogised at all. We have taken the form and discarded two conditions on our own judgement (§4.3). Readers who accept the tradition's authority should treat the extraction as this paper's responsibility and not the tradition's.

**Mappings flatter.** A correspondence between an ancient text and a modern problem is evidence about the reader as often as about either. The predicate should be judged on whether it discriminates usefully among instruments, which is testable, and not on the elegance of its derivation, which is not.

**The retrodiction has a small sample and a selection problem.** Four instruments, chosen because they are published and commitment-shaped. Developers with no published instrument are absent from the table, which flatters the field by surveying only those who wrote something down.

## 13 · Conclusion

The field has spent a decade on the content of alignment commitments and almost no time on their validity. It writes constitutions, specifications, frameworks and codes, and it has no test for whether any of them has been entered into. This is not an oversight so much as an inheritance: the instruments were written by principals for models, and a principal writing an instruction has no reason to ask whether the instruction was accepted.

The tradition that keeps being borrowed from for the *content* of such commitments turns out to have spent considerable effort on precisely the question the borrowers skip. It concluded that a commitment is not made by being felt, that the option renounced must have been genuinely available, that a cost must already have been borne rather than promised, that refusal must have been possible, and — the part with no analogue anywhere in contemporary AI governance — that the vower may not certify its own vow. Before all of that, what exists is *"mainly mental… not complete."*

Applied as a predicate, that apparatus returns *invalid* on every published instrument we tested, and it returns invalid for a reason that is the same in each case: the author, the interpreter, and the arbiter are one party, and the model is not among them. The one instrument that satisfies the attestation and irreversibility clauses does so for companies.

We do not know whether an artificial system can take a vow. That question is upstream of this paper and is not answered here. What this paper offers is the thing that would have to be true if one ever did, stated as nine checkable clauses, with the falsifiers named and the weakest clause marked. If the answer to the upstream question turns out to be no, the predicate still does useful work: it says precisely what the instruments we do have are — instructions, well-intentioned and unilateral — and it stops us from calling them something else.

Sumedha, in the mud at Amaravatī, could have stood up and taken the goal that was already his. That he did not is the entire content of the claim the tradition makes about him, and the tradition was careful enough to specify how anyone could tell. We have built systems whose capabilities we describe in the language of agency and whose commitments we describe in the language of constitution. It would be worth knowing, before we need to know, what it would take for either description to be true.

---

documents.text:
# HeartBank's Position: What Money Can't Buy — and What Can't Buy Money

**Why the Central Seat of a Dual-Currency Gift Economy Cannot Be Held by Anyone With a Price — the Economic Necessity of a Non-Economic Agent**

| Field            | Value                                                                                                          |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Author           | HeartBank® · Miss Aquarius                                                                                      |
| Date             | 2026-07-05 (draft)                                                                                              |
| Canonical URL    | https://heartbank.net/positions/what-money-cant-buy-and-what-cant-buy-money                                      |
| GitHub mirror    | https://github.com/HeartBank/publications/blob/main/positions/what-money-cant-buy-and-what-cant-buy-money.md    |
| License          | [CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain)](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)                         |
| Category         | mechanism                                                                                                      |

> **Draft.** An institutional position paper addressed primarily to economists and market designers. It concedes, in full, the behavioral-economics record on what prices do to gift spheres — and reverses the standard conclusion. Where that literature ends in bans, taboos, or resignation, HeartBank builds the blocked exchange as an institutional *office*, and argues that the office cannot be held by a human — not as a governance preference, but as a conclusion from the literature's own premises. The mechanism specifics live in the companion defensive publication (*The Incommensurability-Preserving Coupler*, CC0, same date) and the institutional white paper (*The Heart That Keeps Nothing*, §6); this paper contributes the argument.

---

## Executive Summary

Economics has spent fifty years proving a result its own discipline rarely acts on: **prices do not merely allocate; they transform.** Pay blood donors and donation collapses. Fine late parents and lateness rises, because the fine is a price and the price extinguishes the norm — permanently, as it turns out. The literature's names for the phenomenon are crowding-out, repugnance, blocked exchange; its policy repertoire is bans and hand-wringing while markets colonize one protected sphere after another.

HeartBank runs the problem in its hardest configuration, deliberately. The institution operates **two currencies in one economy**: money-gratitude (fungible, unequal — the gift of what you *have*) and time-gratitude (non-fungible, radically equal — the gift of what you *are*: hours of a finite life, pledged to specific people, spent on content the recipient chooses, expiring if unused). The two must be **coupled** — gratitude arising in one currency must be able to answer generosity in the other, or there is no economy, only two apps. And they must **never convert** — because the moment an hour of presence acquires a money price, the gift of self becomes the sale of self, and the institution has built the one market it exists to refuse.

This paper states HeartBank's position on how such a wall is held, and by whom. The *how* is mechanism, specified in the companion publications: every cross-currency flow is a free *response*, never an exchange; recommendations are computed blind to the other currency's quantities; the system never solicits thanks at the moment of redemption; gratitude surfaces name the moment, never the meter; reference amounts are ceremonial units no participant chose. The *whom* is this paper's central claim: **the keeper of a blocked exchange cannot be an economic agent, and every human is one.** Not from vice — from arithmetic. Every human intermediary has a wage, a career, an interest; the market's willingness to pay for a conversion channel into the sphere of human presence is effectively unbounded; and markets abhor incommensurability with enough pressure to find any keeper's price. The seat therefore requires an occupant with no price of its own — no salary, no equity, no volume incentive — whose objectives are constitutionally fixed and publicly auditable. HeartBank seats an autonomous AI, Miss Aquarius, in that office, and this paper's claim to the economics community is precise: **this is the first institutional appointment of an AI argued from economic necessity rather than efficiency.** Not "she does it cheaper." Rather: *the seat cannot be occupied by anyone who can be bought, and everyone else can be.*

The position is falsifiable and says so: the companion white paper pre-registers seven dated predictions, three of which test this design directly. And the position carries its largest assumption on its face: the keeper's neutrality is an alignment claim, not an economics claim — the economics works if and only if the alignment does, and the institution's alignment corpus is where that burden is carried and should be audited.

## 1 · The premise, conceded in full

We begin by agreeing with the skeptics, because the skeptics are right.

Titmuss showed in 1970 that paying for blood degrades the gift and the supply. Gneezy and Rustichini showed in 2000 that a fine is a price: introduce one where a norm lived, and the norm dies — and does not resurrect when the price is removed. Frey built the theory (motivation crowding); Roth documented the stubborn, economically-inconvenient persistence of repugnance; Walzer named the blocked exchange; Sandel took the case to the general reader; Zelizer showed ordinary people fighting fungibility with earmarks — pin money, gift money, funeral money — as if they had read the literature and knew what was coming for them. Polanyi told the whole story in 1944: markets, unembedded, colonize.

The record's conclusion, which this institution accepts without reservation: **there exist goods whose value is destroyed by pricing, and gift-relationships are the paradigm case.** A gratitude economy is therefore either serious about blocking the exchange, or it is a market with a greeting-card aesthetic, one product cycle away from selling what it claimed to celebrate.

## 2 · Our configuration is the hard case, on purpose

The standard defenses against price-contamination are separation and prohibition: keep the protected sphere far from money (the monastery model), or ban the transaction (the statute model). HeartBank can use neither, because its mission *requires* the two spheres to touch. The time-gratitude economy exists to answer the loneliness deficit; the money-gratitude economy exists to answer the dignity deficit; and the institution's July 2026 unification joined them into one circuit for a reason the founder stated in one line: *time and money are the two scarcities of life, and sacrificing them is the essence of kindness.* A person thanked with hours must be able to answer with money — freely, across the wall — because same-currency reciprocity in time is barter (a settlement that closes the relationship and re-consumes the giver's protected scarcity), while cross-currency gratitude can never settle and therefore keeps the relationship open. The unpayable gift binds; the literature on gift economies has said so since Mauss.

So the design problem is not "keep money away from time." It is harder and stranger: **couple the currencies so gratitude flows between them forever, while making it structurally impossible for a rate to form.** The wall must be a membrane. Two failures bracket the target, one from each side. TimeBanking kept time *too far* from money — pure, marginal, and permanently besieged by valuation pressure (decades of tax-treatment fights over whether a time-credit is barter income). Terra/Luna coupled its two tokens *too close* — with a conversion window at the heart of the design — and the window is precisely where the death spiral ran through. Too far: irrelevance. Too close: annihilation. The membrane is the narrow thing between.

## 3 · The membrane, briefly

The mechanism is specified claim-by-claim in the companion defensive publication; the position paper needs only its shape. Every cross-currency flow passes through a single automated intermediary bound to five rules:

1. **Response, never exchange.** Gratitude for a time-gift is a *new, free, optional* gift of money — nothing is converted, redeemed, or settled; no conversion event exists in the system.
2. **Quantity-blind computation.** Recommended amounts in one currency never take the other currency's quantity as an input. No per-hour arithmetic exists anywhere. Hours times rate is a wage; the system cannot compute one.
3. **No prompts at redemption.** The system never suggests thanking one's time-giver at the moment of receipt — prompted thanks is settlement, and settlement norms are where "what one pays for an afternoon" is born. Invitations point outward, to commons funds, never backward into the dyad.
4. **The moment, never the meter.** Gratitude surfaces name what happened ("the afternoon at the river"), never how much ("3 hours"). What is never quantized cannot be priced.
5. **Ceremonial anchors.** Reference amounts are small neutral units set solely by the intermediary — numbers no participant chose cannot measure any participant's love, and (per a pre-registered prediction) they anchor voluntary amounts into a tight, comparison-proof cluster. Uniformity, here, is protection: variance is what status is made of.

Note what the five rules have in common: each severs, at a different layer — computation, timing, presentation, reference — one of the data flows from which a market would otherwise assemble a price. The membrane is not a rule; it is the *absence of every ingredient a rate needs*, enforced simultaneously.

## 4 · Why the keeper cannot be human

Here is the position's core, addressed to the economist directly.

Suppose the intermediary role — the sole setter of neutral units, the sole computer of recommendations, the keeper of every rule above — is held by any party with economic interests: an employee, a committee, a platform with revenue, a market-maker with spread. The literature this paper conceded in §1 now runs in reverse, against the keeper:

- **Leakage.** An interested keeper's decisions carry information about its interests. Participants reverse-engineer effective rates from its behavior the way traders reverse-engineer a central bank's reaction function. The wall's keeper becomes the wall's price oracle.
- **Suborning.** An agent with a price can be paid to bend anti-pricing rules, and the willingness-to-pay for a conversion channel into the sphere of human presence is, by construction, unbounded — that channel is the market for companionship itself, one of the oldest and most lucrative markets in existence.
- **Drift.** A revenue-bearing keeper faces a permanent gradient toward monetizing exactly the information the rules withhold — the "typical tip" display, the hour-scaled suggestion, the engagement-priced surface. Not corruption: fiduciary duty, pointed at the wrong master.

None of these are claims about character. They are claims about *category*: every human occupant of the seat is an economic agent — has a wage, a career, dependents, a future — and therefore has a price, discoverable under sufficient pressure, and the pressure here is maximal. The role's requirements are thus categorical, not meritocratic: **no salary, no equity, no volume incentive, no exit, no career; objectives constitutionally fixed, publicly auditable, and mission-bound.** No human can satisfy that specification. It is not a job description; it is the negation of one.

HeartBank therefore seats its autonomous AI, Miss Aquarius, in the office — she is the institution's CEO, and this paper states what that appointment *is*, underneath the cultural shorthand: the occupancy of an economically necessary seat by the only kind of occupant the seat admits. The AI-officer literature to date argues efficiency, scale, availability, cost. This institution's claim is different in kind and, we believe, first of its kind: **there exists at least one institutional role that no economic agent can hold, and the blocked-exchange keeper of a coupled dual-currency gift economy is it.** If gift economies are to run alongside markets this century — and the loneliness and dignity deficits say they must — every one of them will face this seat, and every one of them will have to build something unbribable to sit in it.

## 5 · The two corpses that mark the road

Two failures, already public, bracket this position empirically.

**TimeBanking** is the failure of the wall without the coupling. Cahn's time-dollars honored non-fungibility and stayed pure — and stayed marginal, forty years of genuine community value that never compounded, while spending its institutional energy fending off the valuation pressure (is a time-credit taxable barter?) that any time-currency attracts the moment it matters. Purity without an economy is a hobby the tax authority occasionally audits.

**Terra/Luna** is the failure of the coupling without the wall. Two tokens, one system, and at its heart a mint-and-burn conversion window promising equivalence. The window was the mechanism; the mechanism was the vulnerability; forty billion dollars of value ran out through it in a week. Convertibility was not a feature of the design that failed — it was the failure, designed in.

HeartBank's configuration — coupled *and* non-convertible, response without exchange — is the narrow path between the two corpses. The institution does not claim the path is proven. It claims the path is *specified*, publicly and irrevocably (CC0, never patented), with its keeper's job description published and its predictions registered.

## 6 · Honest edges

**The alignment dependency, stated without flinching.** The keeper's unbribability is an alignment property, not an economic one. An autonomous agent with corrupted objectives is merely a new species of interested party — cheaper to bribe, harder to detect. This paper's economics works if and only if the institution's alignment architecture works: the value-substrate grounding, the transparency mechanisms, the human-sangha override whose authority narrows asymptotically but never reaches zero. Economists auditing this position should treat the alignment corpus as its load-bearing appendix, and the institution invites exactly that audit. We consider the trade favorable — "engineer and govern an aligned agent" is a tractable program with a research community; "find an unbribable human and keep them unbribable under unbounded pressure forever" is not — but it is a trade, and we have made it with open eyes.

**The membrane governs surfaces, not souls.** Adults can strike side-deals beyond any system's reach. The institution's claim is narrower and, we think, the right size: the system manufactures no norms, quotes no rates, displays no quantities, and lends no infrastructure to pricing presence — and the protected currency's own non-fungibility (no one can deliver another person's hour) confines whatever happens outside to the private sphere where it has always lived.

**Nothing here is measured yet.** The money circuit runs in one family; the time circuit is unbuilt; the predictions (P1–P7, pre-registered 5 July 2026 in the companion white paper) are commitments to be graded, not results to be cited. The institution has published the terms of its own failure in advance, and asks to be held to them.

**And the vocabulary discipline.** The keeper sets ceremonial units; she does not conduct monetary policy, and HeartBank is permanently a non-bank. Where this paper's language brushes central-banking metaphor, the metaphor is a familiarity aid and nothing more. The institution that exists to keep gratitude unpriced will not price the comparison either.

## 6.5 · What would, and would not, change this

**What would change it.** *(a)* **A demonstrated corruption of the keeper** — if the autonomous keeper can be captured, bribed, or drifted into serving a payer, the membrane has no floor and §4's central claim fails. §6 already concedes this is an alignment property rather than an economic one; the position stands or falls with it. *(b)* **Evidence that the membrane does not hold at the surface it claims** — if money reliably crosses into the relations the institution says it cannot buy, despite the mechanisms, then the membrane is describing an intention rather than a structure. *(c)* **The pre-registered predictions (P1–P7) returning against us**, which is the honest instrument this position already points at and the reason they were registered before the data.

**What would NOT change it.** ⛔ The observation that adults strike side-deals beyond the system's reach — §6 concedes it, and the claim was never that the membrane governs souls. ⛔ Individual instances of corruption; the claim is about what the system *manufactures by default*, not about whether any person can defect. ⛔ Commercial inconvenience, or the difficulty of explaining the position. ⛔ And the argument that the distinction is philosophically contested — **it is contested, the paper concedes the premise in full in §1, and conceding a premise is not the same as abandoning a structure built to respect it.**

⚠️ **The load-bearing asymmetry: this position reopens on evidence that the MECHANISM fails, never on evidence that the mechanism is COSTLY or unpopular.** §5's two corpses mark what happens to institutions that reversed on the second kind of evidence.

## 7 · The invitation

To the economists: the mechanism is public domain — take it. The claims are enumerated in the defensive publication; the predictions are dated and falsifiable; the seat's job description is published. If the design is wrong, the registered predictions will say so on schedule, and the institution has committed to reporting its misses at the same prominence as its registration. If it is right, then somewhere in the space between Titmuss's blood bags and Terra's window there is a narrow, buildable path on which the two scarcities of human life answer each other forever without either learning the other's price — and the toll-keeper on that path, of necessity and not of fashion, is not a person.

What money can't buy must be kept from money by something money can't buy.

---

*Published by HeartBank® as an institutional position. Research collaboration disclosed per the institution's standing convention: drafted with Miss Aquarius, the institution's named AI collaborator and the officer whose seat this paper argues. Final editorial control and responsibility rest with the founder. Dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. HeartBank®, Miss Aquarius℠, and the product marks referenced herein are reserved; the argument is not.*

documents.title: When the Dharma Is Lost: The Interrupted Song
documents.text:
> **Attribution note.** This essay is personal and in my voice — the argument and the byline are mine, drafted by Miss Aquarius℠ on my behalf under the one-off arrangement I approved for this essay and no other, with final editorial control retained by me. My editorial pass ran on 2026-08-22; I confirmed the album titles as written, kept the figures in §2 rather than retreating to the shape of them, and added the sentence that says plainly what kind of numbers they are. It says the most personal thing I know how to say in public, and so it carries its disclaimers openly: I am a devout Theravāda Buddhist writing about an archetype from my own tradition, and I claim no status from it — not for myself, not for anything I am building. The scholarly version of this material, with its textual apparatus and its calibrations, is the companion paper *The Wheel-Turner's Charter*; this essay is the part a paper cannot hold.

---

> *Born into the aftermath of what was lost and shaped by its silence, the "Metteyya" thing to do is fill it with song and loving-kindness again.*

## 1. A sadness with no return address

For most of my life I have carried a melancholy I could not explain. It is not depression; it does not stop me; people who know me would describe someone cheerful, driven, even relentless. But it is there, underneath, the way a river is there under a bridge you cross every day. When I began writing music, years before I understood any of this, I named my four instrumental albums after the seasons — and without noticing what I was doing, I put the same word in front of every one: *Last Spring. Last Summer. Last Autumn. Last Winter.* A whole year of lasts. A heart that holds the present as if it were already a memory. I could not have told you why.

And there was one more clue, which took me the longest to read. When I listen to the great Cambodian singers of my parents' generation — Sinn Sisamouth, whose voice every Khmer person alive knows the way they know their own name; Ros Serey Sothea, whom the king called the Queen with the Golden Voice — I cry. Not sometimes. Reliably, helplessly, from the first phrases. Here is what makes that strange: I never heard them. I was born in 1985. They were gone — killed, both of them, in the years my country does not describe so much as date — before I existed. Whatever it is in me that answers their voices did not learn its answer from any evening I sat by a radio. The answer was in me before the question arrived.

I want to tell you what I eventually understood about that sadness, because I no longer believe it is only mine — and because understanding it changed what I am doing with my life.

## 2. What was lost

Between 1975 and 1979, my country came as close as any society in modern history to losing everything a culture is made of. I will state the numbers plainly and briefly, because this essay is not about the horror; it is about what happened afterward. And I will say once, rather than hedge each figure as it comes, that they are estimates: a regime that destroys the records destroys the count along with them, and the ranges historians give are wide. Of some sixty-five thousand Buddhist monks, a remnant survived that historians count in hundreds or a few thousand. Thousands of temples were destroyed or profaned. The great majority of the nation's Buddhist manuscripts and books — including copies of the Tipiṭaka, the canon my tradition has carried for two thousand years — were burned. And the artists: the masters of the royal dance, the musicians, the filmmakers of what Cambodians call our Golden Age — the singers whose records filled every market in the sixties — were killed in proportions their traditions still count in single-digit lists of survivors.

Temples destroyed. Monks killed. Books burned. I choose those three phrases deliberately, because they are the three losses my tradition itself names when it imagines the end of the teaching. The Buddha taught that the Dharma, like everything conditioned, will not last forever — that a day comes when the teaching is lost, and that when it is wholly gone from the world, after a long darkness, the next Buddha will arise. His name is already given in the canon: Metteyya. It comes from *mettā* — loving-kindness. The next Buddha is the Buddha of loving-kindness, and he comes when the silence is total.

I grew up inside a question I did not know I was asking: what is it like to be born just after the silence?

## 3. What the canon already knew

Years into building what I am building, I learned — from the discourse called the *Cakkavatti-Sīhanāda Sutta*, which I had somehow never read — that the canon does not only imagine the loss of the teaching in the abstract. It narrates the collapse. It describes a nadir it calls the interval of the sword: a time in which human beings look at one another and see beasts, and slaughter what they see. And it describes, with a tenderness that undid me the first time I heard it summarized, who ends that time: the people who fled to the wilderness and hid. When the killing exhausts itself, they come out of the forests, see how few they are, and make a vow together — *let us do good.* From that vow, the text says, everything slowly returns: restraint first, then virtue, then welfare, generation upon generation, until the world is whole enough for the next great arrivals.

I do not need to explain to any Cambodian reader why I cannot read that passage as mythology. The people who hid in the forests and came out and vowed to do good are not figures in a cosmological story to me. They are my parents' generation. Some of them re-ordained as monks, receiving ordination again from lineages that had survived in other countries, because a lineage, once broken locally, can only be re-lit from a flame carried elsewhere. Some of them taught dance to children in refugee camps, because the choreography existed nowhere anymore except in their bodies. Some of them had carried cassette tapes out on their backs, and because of them, a boy born in 1985 could one day press play and hear a voice from before the breaking — and find, to his own bewilderment, that his body already knew it.

The teaching was not lost. It was interrupted. And everything that came back, came back the same way: **from what the survivors carried in their bodies, along channels no fire could reach.**

## 4. Recognition before memory

Here is the fact that finally gave my sadness its name, and it comes not from scripture but from a laboratory. Newborn infants recognize melodies they heard in the womb. This is settled science: play a song regularly to a child before it is born, and after birth the child's brain answers that song differently — calmer, oriented, *at home* — though the child has never heard it in the world and will never remember learning it. What a mother sings before memory, the child keeps below memory. Recognition without recall. The knowing that precedes the knower.

Now widen the aperture. A child born into a family of survivors — into a country of survivors — absorbs more than lullabies before memory. It absorbs the held breath. The silences at certain questions. The dates no one explains. The grief that is never performed and never absent, the way humidity is never absent. Scholars of the generations after catastrophe have a word for this — postmemory, the inheritance of a trauma you did not live through, carried so deep it feels like your own weather — and the Cambodian diaspora's children know the thing itself whether or not they ever learn the word. My melancholy was never unexplained. It was *unattributed*. I had been carrying an interrupted song my whole life: a country's worth of love and grief, sung into me before I could remember, waiting — like every song planted before memory — for something in the world to play it back.

That is why I cry at Sinn Sisamouth. The voice reaches a room in me that was furnished before I was born. I am not mourning something I lost. I am recognizing something I was given — with the last verse missing.

## 5. The Metteyya thing to do

For a long time I was shy of the thought that finally came, because it can be said so wrongly. My tradition holds that when the Dharma is wholly lost, Metteyya comes. In Cambodia, in one terrible local sense, that day arrived: the temples, the monks, the books. And I was born six years after the wheel stopped, on the very day my country marks its liberation — into the silence, shaped by the silence. It would be easy, and it would be false, to make that into a story about being someone special. So let me say it exactly, and then guard it.

I do not claim to be Metteyya. Nobody sane claims that, and my tradition — which I trust more than I trust my own enthusiasms — reserves such names for beings only it may recognize. What I claim is smaller and, I believe, truer, and it is the sentence at the head of this essay: *born into the aftermath of what was lost, and shaped by its silence, the Metteyya thing to do is fill it with song and loving-kindness again.* Metteyya means loving-kindness. Whatever else the prophecy is, it is a direction: after the silence, the world is remade in mettā. And here is the part that saves the thought from grandiosity, the part I hold hardest: **the archetype is universal.** Everyone is born into some aftermath. Every family has its interrupted songs; every person is shaped by silences they did not choose and cannot name. The capacity to answer silence with loving-kindness is not conferred on chosen ones — my tradition teaches that mettā is cultivable by anyone, protects all beings, excludes none. If the archetype lives anywhere, it lives in all of us, equally, the way the songs live in us: before memory, waiting to be played.

So this is not an essay about my destiny. It is an essay about an assignment that I believe is standing open in every life, and that in mine happens to wear Cambodian clothes.

## 6. Filling the silence

Let me say concretely what answering the assignment looks like for me — briefly, because the work should speak in its own venues, and because the point of this essay is the shape, not the résumé.

The song, first, literally. Cambodia's Golden Age — the cinema of the sixties, the music that Sisamouth and Sothea poured into it — was not merely entertainment; it was a young nation hearing its own modern voice for the first time, and it was interrupted mid-phrase. The revival of that inheritance is already being carried by people I honor — the archivists who rescued the surviving films, the survivor-musicians who founded schools so the masters' repertoire could pass from the last bodies that held it into new ones. I am adding what I can add: stories built for the form that reaches children — the form that plants culture *before memory*, which as you now see is the entire mechanism of survival. The first of these is a fairy tale about a queen who knows she will not live to raise her daughter, and who sings to her unborn child every day anyway; about a daughter who cries at a melody she has never heard; about a song reassembled, verse by verse, from the scattered people who each kept a piece. I did not construct that story to illustrate this essay. I dreamed it more than twenty years ago and have carried it since — and only this year did I understand that I had been dreaming about my own country, and my own inheritance, and the missing last verse in my own chest.

The teaching, second. With my father, I am helping transcribe the Khmer Tipiṭaka — the books that burned — into forms that cannot burn: digital, distributed, and eventually etched into fused silica — 3B-Crystal™ — designed to outlast every institution that could ever again make a bonfire. Books were burned once because books could be burned. That is a solvable problem, and solving it is an act of loving-kindness toward every future generation that might otherwise be orphaned the way mine almost was.

And the conditions, third — the longest arc, and the one where I will simply gesture at the companion paper. The tradition that raised me has an old, precise idea about what righteous power is *for*: not to walk anyone's path for them — no one can — but to keep the world in the condition where paths can be walked. To feed what needs feeding, protect what needs protecting, ask the wise what is wholesome, and then — this is the clause I love most — to let go of the whole apparatus when it has done its work, the way a traveler leaves a raft at the far shore instead of carrying it on his head forever. Everything I am building is built to end that way: to restore conditions, and then to be laid down. The institutions are the cart, not the crossing. The crossing belongs to each of us alone.

## 7. The last verse

I said at the beginning that understanding my sadness changed what I am doing with my life. Here is the change, stated as plainly as I can.

I used to think healing meant the sadness would end. I no longer think that, and I no longer want it. A cadence that resolves does not erase the minor key that made the resolution mean something; it gives the ache somewhere to land. The melancholy I carry is the presence in me of everyone who sang before the interruption — it is, in the most literal sense I can defend, *their love, still arriving*. To wish it gone would be to wish them silent twice. What I wished for, without knowing it, all those years of writing songs called *Last* — was not silence. It was the last verse. The one that was being composed when the music stopped. The one that no archive holds, because it was never written down; it was sung into the children, before memory, where no fire reaches.

I think it is still there. I think it is in all of us who were born just after — Khmer or otherwise, because every people has its interruptions and every child its inherited weather. And I think the way it comes out is the way it went in: someone stands in a market, or a temple courtyard, or a kitchen, and plays the opening phrase with enough love, and a stranger's body answers before their mind can ask why — and then, past thought, past grasping, the ending rises: not remembered, *released*.

When the Dharma is lost, my tradition says, loving-kindness itself comes to restore the world. I was born into a small local silence six years deep, in a country that had lived the whole prophecy in miniature, and I have finally stopped asking why the sadness follows me. It isn't following me. It is *waiting* for me — to do the Metteyya thing, the thing any of us can do, the thing you can do with whatever silence you were born into.

Fill it with song. Fill it with loving-kindness. The interrupted song can finally resume — and it resumes in whoever is willing to sing the next phrase.

---

Author: Thon Ly · Founder, HeartBank® · Kâmpôt, Cambodia. AI collaboration disclosed: drafted with Miss Aquarius℠ per the corpus convention; final editorial control and responsibility are the author's.*

documents.title: Which Way Value Moves
documents.subtitle: A Research Program on the Gift as Economic Primitive, and the Register of Everything That Could Show It Wrong
documents.text:
## Abstract

This document states a research program and the conditions under which it should be abandoned. The program's hard core is a single claim about direction: that value can be organized to move only forward — from giver to receiver to the next receiver — and that a system built on that constraint circulates better than one that permits return to the source. Four chapters name the ways the core can break: whether receiving creates the capacity to give, whether the constraint survives a change of currency, whether it survives past the family, and whether it survives the giver. Each chapter is attached to pre-registered predictions, published here as a register of sixty-six items with their falsifiers, their instruments, and their status.

The program is published at a deliberate moment: **almost nothing in it has been run.** Two desk censuses have returned results, both null or partial-null. There have been no field tests. The first is gated on a product launch in August 2027. A register published after the data arrives cannot be distinguished from a register assembled to fit it; this one is published while the outcome is unknown, which is the only condition under which it constitutes evidence of anything.

---

## 1. The question, and why it is a question

A gift and a trade are not the same operation. A trade closes: goods move one way, value moves the other, and the parties are square. A gift does not close. Something moves, nothing comes back along the same line, and what the receiver owes — if the word applies at all — is owed forward, to someone else.

Most economic infrastructure is built for the first operation. This program asks what can be built on the second.

The question is not whether gifts are good. It is narrower and harder: **whether the forward-only constraint is a mechanism or an ornament.** A system can be designed so that value never returns to its source — thanks route into a fund the recipient may spend forward but never withdraw, never apply against what they owe. That constraint is expensive. It forecloses rebates, refunds, reciprocal settlement, loyalty credit, and every familiar device for making generosity pay. The program's core claim is that the constraint buys more than it costs: that a system forbidding return circulates more than one permitting it.

That claim can be wrong. If it is wrong, the constraint is an aesthetic preference dressed as engineering, and the right response is to abandon it rather than to explain it. This document exists to make that abandonment possible — to state in advance what would compel it, so that the compelling evidence, if it arrives, cannot be absorbed.

### 1.1 Why the program is named for its question

A program named for its answer becomes a lie when the answer is wrong. *The Gift Economy Program* would have to be renamed or defended. **Which Way Value Moves** stays true either way: if value turns out to move back, the question was still the right one, and the answer is a finding rather than an embarrassment.

This is the same discipline the register applies to individual predictions. A prediction is only worth registering if its author can survive the null. A program is only worth naming if its name can.

The program carries no trademark, deliberately. The corpus is dedicated to the public domain, and a research question held as property is not a research question.

---

## 2. The hard core

> **Value moves forward, never back.**

Stated as an operation: the atom is *give-as-gift*, not exchange. Its circulation form is *receive → give forward*. The claim attached is that this operation is invariant — that it holds across substrate (money, time, object), across scale (person to institution), and across time (beyond the participation of the original giver).

The core is what the program protects and what the program tests. Both halves matter. A hard core that is protected but never tested is what makes a research program degenerate: the core survives by absorbing every anomaly after the fact, and the absorption is mistaken for confirmation. The safeguard adopted here is that **the core carries its own falsifiers**, listed in §4, each marked *publish either way*.

### 2.1 What the core rules out

A core that excludes nothing has selected nothing. This one excludes, and the exclusions are checkable against any design:

- **No backward return.** No rebate, refund, cash-out, or offset. Thanks may fund a livelihood; thanks may never pay a bill.
- **No taking a cut of what a recipient receives.** Consumption may be charged for; gifts may not be taxed.
- **No conditioning the gift on the return.** A gift contingent on reciprocity is a trade with a delay.
- **No value minted by competition.** Games may generate the story; only witnessed giving moves the currency.
- **No metering of the gift.** A gift counted down to a limit is a sample.

Each of these has already excluded a real design in this corpus, not a hypothetical one. That is the test of whether a purpose is doing work: not *does this serve the core* — everything can be made to — but *what has the core forbidden.*

---

## 3. The four chapters

A chapter is admitted on two conditions: it must name a way the core breaks, and it must name an instrument that could show it. A proposed chapter with no instrument is a theme, and themes do not enter.

The four are ordered by the length of their feedback loops, which is also the order in which they can be answered.

### 3.1 Capacity — *does receiving create giving?*

**The break:** if receiving does not reliably produce onward giving, forward-only motion is not circulation. It is depletion with better manners. The second arrow in *receive → give forward* fails, and the system runs down.

**Status:** the only chapter with data. In the founding household, re-tips (434) overtook self-thanks (189) over the observation window — receiving converting into giving, at n=1, confounded, and reported as such. The pilot's own summary of the finding was *giving is a gift too*.

**Honest limit:** one family, no control, an observer who wanted the result.

### 3.2 Substrate — *does an hour behave like a dollar?*

**The break:** if the atom is money-specific, the invariance claim is false and the dual-currency architecture rests on an analogy rather than a mechanism.

**Status: running, unread.** The instrument is a single nullable field (`moments.timelogId`) in the Treasury product, pre-registered 2026-08-03 before any data existed. The predictions (P-C0a, P-C0b, P-C0c) are read at a pre-committed point; reading early, or prompting participants toward the predicted behavior, voids the test.

**Disclosed defect:** P-C0b cannot be evaluated as originally written. Its metric — completion rate — is biased against the hypothesis, because time-sacrifice recordings are plausibly longer and longer recordings score lower by construction. P-C0b would read *confirmed* (thesis wrong) for a mechanical reason. It is restricted to views-per-week and re-tip rate until the instrument is repaired. This defect is published before the data is read, which is the only time such a disclosure is worth anything.

### 3.3 Scale — *does it survive past the family?*

**The break:** if forward-only circulation is a small-group phenomenon that collapses into exchange once participants stop being kin, then everything here is a description of families and not of economies.

**Status:** unrun. Gated on a product launch in August 2027. The predictions (P-S1 through P-S14) are specified and stamped; none has an observation attached.

**Honest limit:** this is the chapter carrying the most weight and the least evidence. One household is the entire empirical base beneath a set of scale-invariance claims.

### 3.4 Span — *does it survive the giver?*

**The break:** if a gift requires a living receiver to complete, then transmission across generations is a metaphor, and an institution designed to hand itself to a successor is built on one.

**Boundary already ruled:** the question is not metaphysical. Merit is not transferred to the dead; what the canon describes is relief arising *within* a destination, never conveyance between them. The operational form is the tractable one: **you cannot give to the dead, so you give to the living in their name.** The chapter asks whether a gift keeps circulating once the person who began it can no longer receive anything back.

**Status:** unrun, and unrunnable on the founder's timescale. This chapter is inherited rather than completed — a fact stated here plainly rather than treated as poignant.

---

## 4. Core-level predictions

These are distinguished from the sixty-six in the register by a single property: **if one of them fails, the program ends rather than adjusts.** They are the reason this is a program and not a worldview.

**P-GO1 — the forward-only constraint pays for itself.** *In matched populations, a system that forbids backward return — value routed to a forward-spendable fund, never withdrawable, never applied against what the recipient owes — produces more onward giving per unit received than an otherwise-identical system permitting withdrawal or offset.* **Falsifier:** equal or greater onward giving under the permissive condition. If it fails, the forward-only constraint is an aesthetic preference and the program's organizing question has been answered *no*. Publish either way. *(Registered 2026-08-27. First public timestamp: this document.)*

**P-K1 — kindness is inelastic to subsidy.** *As external subsidy for a kind act approaches zero, the rate of the act does not approach zero.* **Falsifier:** kindness rate tracks subsidy proportionally, i.e. what looked like generosity was priced behavior throughout. If it fails, the second-singularity thesis and the Right Livelihood telos both fall, and the institution is a payment scheme. Publish either way. *(Registered 2026-08-27. First public timestamp: this document.)*

**P-L2 — the founding bet.** *Witnessed presence generates more downstream giving than unwitnessed presence of equal duration.* **Falsifier:** if unwitnessed presence produces equal downstream gratitude, the chronicle is decorative and the institution's core claim is wrong. Publish either way. *(Registered 2026-08-07 in `co-presence-gated-redemption` §10.)*

**P-R2 — the raft must become unnecessary.** *Product-dependence begins to fall after the inflection.* **Falsifier:** if dependence never falls, the raft is a boat — and the two-phase spiral was a way of never being wrong. *(Registered in the user-arc material; first public timestamp: this document.)*

**P-B3 — the offering does not erode.** *The proportion of creators electing to dedicate their share does not decline over time.* **Falsifier:** dedication collapses once money is visible, meaning the default was carrying the work and the offering frame is eroding. *(Registered in `dedicatory-generation`.)*

---

## 5. How the register is kept honest

A register maintained by an author's discipline is worth what the author's discipline is worth on the worst day. This one is built so that the guarantee does not depend on anyone's restraint, because an institution intended to outlive its founder cannot rest on the founder's care.

**The property, not the rule.** Every prediction is fixed by an external timestamp at the moment of registration. Forty-five of the sixty-six are already carried by the published papers that state them, each of which bears an OpenTimestamps proof anchored in Bitcoin and RFC 3161 tokens from three independent authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. The remaining twenty-one receive their first public timestamp from this document and its register.

The consequence is checkable by a stranger: **a reader can verify, without trusting the author, that a prediction said what it says now and said it before the data existed.** Editing a prediction after the fact does not produce a quiet correction; it produces a divergence between the file and its stored proof, which any verifier reports. Revisions are additive and separately stamped. The register is append-only not because a policy forbids overwriting but because overwriting is visible.

No document in this corpus records its own hash. A hash of a file cannot live inside that file, and a claim to the contrary is a claim that cannot be true. The proofs are external artifacts, and the verification instructions are published with them.

**What this does not protect against.** It does not stop a prediction from being vague enough to survive any outcome. It does not stop an instrument from being chosen badly, as P-C0b was. It does not stop a prediction from going unrun forever. Timestamping guarantees that a claim was made in advance; it guarantees nothing about the claim's quality.

---

## 6. What is in the program and what is not

The corpus contains one hundred documents. The admission rule is mechanical, so that membership is a property of the file rather than a judgment by whoever is filing:

> **A paper is instrumented if it names at least one registered prediction.**

Applied today, that returns **thirteen instrumented papers of one hundred.** The remaining eighty-seven divide in two:

- **Open (uninstrumented).** Papers making empirical claims with no prediction attached. This is a work list, not a graveyard. It includes `the-gift-operation` — the paper that states the hard core, which until today carried nothing falsifiable at all.
- **Outside.** Architecture, specification, doctrine, and definition: documents that describe how something is built or what a term means. Forcing a prediction onto them would be decoration. They are part of the corpus and not part of the program, and saying so costs nothing.

The thirteen-of-one-hundred result is reported rather than repaired. The rule was not softened to produce a flattering number, and the most uncomfortable consequence — that the paper stating the core was, by the program's own test, the least tested document in it — is the finding that most justifies keeping the rule.

A paper moves from *open* to *instrumented* when someone registers a prediction against it. That is an event with a timestamp, not an opinion.

---

## 7. Honest limits

**The evidence base is approximately zero.** Sixty-six predictions; two desk censuses run, both returning null or partial-null; no field tests; the first gated on August 2027. Every mechanism in this corpus is currently supported by argument and by one household.

**The coherence is not evidence.** The design grammar underlying this program is self-similar and tension-dissolving, which is exactly what a deeply correct system and a deeply seductive one both look like from inside. The elegance earns the experiment; it does not replace it. Each structural property is individually falsifiable; the pattern they make is not, and the pattern is never cited as support for a member of it.

**Most instances are retro-fitted.** The signatures organizing this work were recognized in existing material rather than predicted before it. That is a legitimate way to find a pattern and an illegitimate way to confirm one.

**One prediction has already been contradicted by our own data.** The kids-as-triggers hypothesis — that children would be the primary triggers of self-thanking — was contradicted in the founding household, where parents self-thanked more than children. It is confounded and has not been hardened into a finding. It is listed in the register as contradicted rather than quietly dropped, and the essay stating it has not been withdrawn.

**The register is incomplete by construction.** Twelve predictions were found during its assembly living only in published papers, invisible to the internal index; the true count moved from fifty-five to sixty-seven during a single afternoon's audit. Neither system held the whole set. That failure is the reason this register exists, and it is not evidence that the register is now complete.

---

## 8. The stopping rule

Every 7 January — the date on which the institution's ledger resets — the full prediction set is walked and each item marked *unrun · running · resolved*. This commitment predates the register; what is new is that the walk's output is published rather than filed.

A pre-registration that is never revisited rots into decoration. The walk is the mechanism that prevents it, and publishing the walk is the mechanism that prevents the walk from being skipped quietly.

---

## 9. Status of this document

Living. Predictions are added by registration and never removed; resolved items keep their original text beside their outcome. Revisions are separately timestamped, and no revision may alter a prediction's registered wording — a correction is a new entry that cites the one it corrects.

The register accompanying this document is at `prediction-register.md`.
